BUSINESS OF SUPPLY ALLOTTED DAY S O. 62-TECHNOLOGICAL CHANGE
speechtext:
That this House condemns the Government for its failure to work co-operatively with the provinces, business, labour, voluntary organizations and the educational community to provide adequate training and retraining opportunities that would enable Canadian workers to feel confident about their ability to deal with the challenges of rapid technological change.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to stand in the House today and devote a full day of the time of the House to what I think may be the most important problem in the country which must be resolved if we are to have an economic future that is full of opportunity and hope for Canadians.
The Conservative task force which dealt with technological change, manpower training and retraining has concluded that those who tell us that the country will require two million new jobs by 1990 simply to retain today's unemployment rate are correct. We find ourselves in an era of rapid change. We on this side of the House have spoken many, many times about the fact that there are well over half a million young people in Canada today who are unemployed. What has not been said with enough frequency is that 73 per cent of those unemployed young Canadians have not been educated or trained beyond high school. In many cases, unemployed young Canadians have not even completed high school.
The fact that unemployed young people are not being trained beyond high school and that within six years we must find two million new jobs within the Canadian economy underlie the thesis advanced by the Conservative Party task force report. When those two facts are coupled with an awareness of the fact that 90 per cent of the people who will be employed in 1990 are already employed in the Canadian economy, we then begin to understand the degree to which we should already have embarked upon a priority program for the training and education of adults. Our failure to do so is inexcusable.
I brought with me today reports which have been prepared in the last four or five years which deal with this issue. At the top of the pile of these reports is a report entitled In the Chips, Opportunities for People Partnerships. That report was put
out by the federal Department of Labour. I was vice-chairman when a report entitled Work for Tomorrow, a report of one of the first task forces set up by Parliament to study the issue of the Canadian work force and its needs for training and retraining, was made. That task force reported to the House over three years ago with well over 200 recommendations. However, the Government is very good at appointing task forces and study groups and employing consultants to provide it with answers and policy proposals, but it does not pay any attention to such things.
The next major report I have with me is in two volumes and is entitled Learning a Living in Canada. What has been done about that report, Mr. Speaker? I have with me a very recent report entitled Learning for Life. What has the Government done about that report? What has it done about the report of the Canadian Adult Education Association entitled Prom the Adult's Point of View, What Should We Do About Education? I have as well a report entitled A Working Majority, What Women Must Do for Pay. I have listed just a sample of the total number of reports and studies which have been produced in the 1980s containing advice for the Government. Nothing has been done about these reports.
It is particularly galling to see on the news or in the newspapers night after night leadership candidates like the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Roberts) talking about the need to use unemployment insurance funds for training. The Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Johnston) has indicated that he has similar views. Those ideas were given to the Government well over three years ago by an all-Party committee of the House of Commons. When that advice was given to the Government, the committee also indicated that the need was urgent. Three years ago the need was urgent, and now we are into the spring of 1984 and the Government has done nothing about it.

The Minister of Employment and Immigration, a leadership candidate, rose in the House last week and said that any idea of the Conservative task force which was not already in place was regressive and startling. That told us more about the Minister and his knowledge of his Department and the advice given to it than anything else. That same Minister stood in the House and told us that $1 billion of unemployment insurance funds were going into the pockets of people so that they could take training, when the Main Estimates indicated $250 million or a quarter of that amount, and that the Government had the intention of cutting unemployment insurance funds for people to take training. To have the Minister stand in the House and tell us the opposite speaks volumes about the competence of

the Minister, the concern of the Minister and of the entire Cabinet. The ideas have been around for years. To this day the Minister gives us no indication that he understands those ideas or that he has a legitimate committee to the actualization of those ideas.
What about the educational challenge of the future? Those of us who serve society in the capacity of Members of Parliament of whatever political Party, those of us who have constituency offices in our neighbourhoods and communities, are in touch with unemployed Canadians. They telephone us and they come to see us. Many of them have a rather consistent history of unemployment which goes back a good many years. The common characteristic of those people is that they are not particularly well trained or well educated. Statistics Canada and OECD tell us that somewhere between 27 per cent and 30 per cent of the labour force in the country are functionally illiterate. They cannot read or write well enough to participate fully in training for the modern age. That is a large part of the problem of those who have experienced a great deal of unemployment in the last 10 years to 20 years.
Every Member of Parliament who serves in this Chamber is meeting with unemployed Canadians who have a lot of education, who have obtained master's degrees or doctorates, who have been engineers with 20 years of experience. They are family people with mortgages, car payments and all the obligations which are characteristic of people who have been successful in the labour force for 10, 15 and 20 years. It is those kinds of Canadians who represent the increase in unemployment. Personal anguish is always part of finding themselves suddenly or unexpectedly unemployed. It is that kind of personal anguish which produces statistics such as the following: that every 1 per cent increase in unemployment in society produces a 5 per cent increase in stress-related diseases such as heart attacks, alcoholism, suicide, severe depression and mental illness.
In the life of this Government over the last four years, the unemployment rate has been hiked by 4 per cent to 5 per cent. That tells us, Mr. Speaker, that there is a 20 per cent to 25 per cent increase in stress-related illness in this country as a direct consequence of unemployment. What do we say to those unemployed people today? We tell them that they can collect their unemployment insurance cheque, but do we tell them that while they are collecting that cheque, in a climate where jobs do not exist they can go to school and upgrade their skills? Do we tell them to prepare themselves for the jobs of the future? As a society, Mr. Speaker, we do not, and I suggest to you that it is time we did.
In our Canadian society we must begin to treat the utilization of social expenditures as an investment in people, as a necessary investment, as a wise investment and as a compassionate investment. We must begin to invest in people so they can have a sense of hope about the future. That is the first major shift in public policy which our Party is calling for.
I would like to contrast the Canadian experience with the Japanese experience for just a moment. One of the research findings in the world today is that the average Japanese adult scores ten points higher on an intelligence test than the average North American adult. Does that tell us that there is a genetic difference? I suggest to you that it does not. However, it tells us a great deal about the Japanese culture and its commitment to the educational process. In a nation like Japan, Mr. Speaker, when the economy goes down a little and there is less need for people to do the jobs, the Japanese people go into further training. They are not laid off or put out on the street. They are not told to sit at home and apply for jobs three times a week. They are encouraged to learn something more than they already know. That pays off across their whole society. When we look at the Japanese economy today and we see that it is healthy, that its unemployment and inflation rates are lower, and that it is succeeding in an increasingly competitive world market, we do not have to look much beyond the commitment to education and training to find a reason for its success.
I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that there are five changes in public policy indicated in this country. We should make those changes as quickly as possible and with as much strength and vigour as we can muster.
The first change, Mr. Speaker, is to increase educational consumerism. We have to change the tax system to make it as desirable to invest in people as it currently is to invest in property, machinery and buildings. Surely, Mr. Speaker, the strength of this nation is in its people. Nothing is built, nothing happens in the economy, without well trained, committed, motivated and skilled people. We must examine every piece of public policy with a view to directing our efforts towards increasing educational consumerism, the willingness of people to participate in educational processes.
Second, Mr. Speaker, we have to use these social assistance and spending programs to support adults in the pursuit of knowledge, in training and retraining. They need income help to make their mortgage and car payments while they participate in training.
Third, we have to move beyond our dependence on the public sector to be the sole provider of educational opportunity and encourage the private and non-profit sectors generally to become more active and more involved in the provision of knowledge. They can then pass on their knowledge to succeeding generations, young and old.
The fourth plank, Mr. Speaker, is to provide special support to those with the inclination and background which enables them to fill jobs dedicated and devoted to the creation of knowledge itself, those of technicians, scientists and so on. We talked about this as a commitment to research. If you conceive it broadly, then we are on the right track. But looking ahead to the creation of the two million jobs necessary, no one knows what they are going to be. We do know, however, that it is human creativity and inventiveness, built on human skills and

knowledge, which will produce those new products and services to employ Canadians who are looking eagerly for work. Therefore, the fourth plank is commitment to the creation of new knowledge and we must move quickly on that.
The fifth plank, Mr. Speaker, is really what I think of in a sense as an energy resolution. We waste so much energy in this nation of ours in confrontation between governments, between governments and labour, business and labour, and business and government. We have to re-examine many of the institutions in our society, always with the view to reducing confrontation and increasing co-operation. We will not solve major problems, in particular the training problem, we will not make the massive commitment necessary to training and retraining of our labour force, in the absence of an attitude characterized by co-operation rather than confrontation.
Throughout this day, Mr. Speaker, a number of Members from our Caucus will be standing in this Chamber and speaking to the issue we have identified in our motion. If I can just read it one last time before I sit down, it says:
That this House condemns the Government for its failure to work co-operatively with the provinces, business, labour, voluntary organizations and the educational community to provide adequate training and retraining opportunities that would enable Canadian workers to feel confident about their ability to deal with the challenges of rapid technological change.
Mr. Speaker, a recent survey in Canada told us that 40 per cent of Canadian firms are experiencing difficulty today in hiring people with the proper training to do the job. In a country where measured unemployment is 1.5 million people and true unemployment is two million people, we have jobs going begging because Canadians do not have the necessary skills to fill them. This is a national tragedy; however, it is solvable. I suggest to Members that as the day goes along it would be worthwhile to put on the table their ideas as to what we should be doing to solve that problem.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to participate in this opposition day debate. I want to commend the Conservatives for choosing this topic. I think it is important that this topic has been chosen for debate today because it is a crucial concern of all Canadians. The Official Opposition's motion calls upon us to pay attention to retraining as it affects the opportunities or lack of opportunities resulting from technological change. Although it is important to focus attention upon training and retraining as a result of the technological change that we are going through today, obviously a focus on training only is not sufficient. If we are going to train people we must ensure there will be jobs for people once they have the training.
Technological change, Mr. Speaker, does not only involve a few computer or software companies in the Ottawa valley or other kinds of high-tech industries being introduced into the Canadian economy. Technological change is an all-pervasive
Supply
phenomenon that affects every institution, industry and sector of Canadian society. It is affecting the old and established industries which need to be retooled. It is a cause for the emergence of new industries and for a reshaping of the whole economy which involves a growth in the service sector.
Technological change promises the creation of new wealth. It is this promise of new wealth that is at the core of how we approach technological change. If this new wealth is simply going to be for the few, it is going to lead to continued polarization of society and continued injustice and we will be left with large numbers of people unemployed. We must address the question of the distribution of wealth that results from technological change.
One of the ways of approaching this is to look at it from the perspective of job creation and employment. Up until now technological change has resulted in massive job loss. Most of the studies which deal with technological change indicate that there will be more of this in the future. We must ask ourselves how we can assure that all Canadians have employment as we go through this period of technological change and job loss.
One of the concrete ways, Mr. Speaker, of assuring the fair distribution of wealth and jobs is to put greater priority on the concept of the introduction of a shorter work week. If technological change is going to produce greater wealth and raise the productivity of our economy, it should be possible within that framework to reduce the length of the work week. There would, therefore, be more people employed and the people who would otherwise be unemployed would not be bearing the burden of technological change.
However, moving toward a shorter work week will not solve the unemployment problems that will result from the social change that is occurring in our society right now. We will have very seriously to consider how we can create vast numbers of new jobs. One sector in which we can create new employment is human resources, whether as part of the Public Service or the volunteer sector. It is important to begin paying decent wages to people in these sectors. This includes people who work in daycares and those who take care of senior citizens in senior citizen homes, nursing homes or by assisting with chores that seniors cannot handle on their own.
Of course, in order adequately to compensate these people and ensure that enough are doing these jobs, it is necessary to find the money to pay for those services. I suggest this money should come from the increment in wealth that is promised as a result of technological change. Those companies which have increased productivity and therefore a greater share of markets, greater wealth and income should pay a fair share of the tax burden in this country so that we can see that human needs are being met and that our people are employed.
Fair distribution of wealth as a result of technological change brings into question the whole issue of fair taxation. It is a well known fact that over the last couple of decades in this country the burden of taxation has shifted from the corporate sector to the individual. The system for individual income tax

is so riddled with loopholes that it is no longer the progressive taxation system that it should be. These many loopholes in the taxation system permit people who earn over $100,000 a year to pay no income tax while the very poor people are faced with a heavy taxation burden. An important part of dealing with technological change in the future concerns implementing a fair taxation system.
Technological change also involves a great adjustment for workers. In order for people humanely to adapt to this change, it is necessary that a number of policy changes take place. For example, when new technology is introduced into an industry, it is important that consultation should take place with the workers so that they are involved in the decision-making concerning the introduction of new technology. The decision for these changes should not be left solely to the individual manager in particular industries; the involvement of workers must be enshrined in legislation. Furthermore, those who will be affected by technological change should be given sufficient notice of this change so that they can prepare for that adjustment.
We must ensure that when workers are laid off as a result of technological change, there are adequate severance pay provisions because the provisions now in place are simply inadequate to deal with the massive technological change that we are experiencing today.
Training is another element of technological change and social adjustment which people must face. Those who lose their jobs because of technological change must have adequate training so they can move into new employment that provides them with a fair and equitable lifestyle and income. In other words, people who are displaced by technology should not have to leave a good-paying job for a low-paying position. They should be ensured of a fair share of the wealth which will eventually come to our society with these changes. This can be assured by adequate training.
There have been a number of proposals for increasing the amount of training in Canada, particularly with respect to the private sector. Let me focus my attention on this subject. A recent report recommended the introduction of paid educational leave. This is an important step for Canadian society to take. It would allow employees to accumulate the right to a certain amount of training, depending on how long they have worked in the industry. Such a program would encourage industry to support the training system in Canada. This is a necessary step, given the over-all record of inadequate training in this country compared to that which takes place in Europe, for example.
Paid educational leave could also alleviate one of the fundamental social problems we face today, which is the serious problem of functional illiteracy. Many people today simply do not have adequate literacy skills in order to function in a modern industrial economy. This recommendation must be considered not only in the context of a productive economy but also from the point of view of social justice. There is no way that those who are functionally illiterate can participate fairly in the wealth of our society.
Women have already been severely affected by technological change and will continue to be affected by this change in the future. Women already suffer inequality since they currently earn approximately 60 per cent of what men earn in similar employment. Since technological change will affect those industries which predominantly employ women, this inequality will increase rather than decrease the difference between their wages with men unless deliberate steps are taken to give them adequate training. These women must have specific training programs to which they have adequate access so that they can share in the wealth that is produced by our economy.
Women are not the only minority group that requires training for our changing economy. The recent report entitled Equality Now focused attention on visible minorities. A productive society which produces wealth must assume social peace and consensus. This can take place only when everyone is treated justly, which cannot happen if some are excluded from sharing in the benefits of our society. The visible minorities require specific strategies in order to have access to the mainstream of Canadian society and good jobs. This requires an affirmative action approach to visible minorities.
Today we have unprecedented numbers of young people who are unemployed, who really have come to the conclusion that they have no hope for the future with regard to employment. Our training endeavours must include them. If we simply abandon a generation of young Canadians to a hopeless situation, then we are setting a time bomb for Canadian society in the future.
When I first started speaking, I mentioned that it was not sufficient to focus upon training alone. When we think in terms of adjustment, we have to think not simply in terms of the adjustment of individual workers but also in terms of the adjustment of the economy as a whole. We need to put in place an industrial strategy to see that we get a fair share of tomorrow's markets, and as technological change sweeps through our economy we must see that we have strong and productive industries. This cannot occur simply by happenstance. Nor can it happen if we leave it to the private market alone. We have to plan the ways in which we are going to ensure that Canadians produce the goods to meet the domestic needs we have and that we can produce goods in a way that allows us to have an adequate penetration into international markets.
We have to plan policies for adjusting the Canadian economy not just with the objective of economic growth but also in the context of full employment. We must aim all of our instruments of public policy at the objective of providing jobs for all Canadians. If we are going to put in place adequate training, then we have to ask, training for what? Therefore we have to plan for those jobs which have to be in place if technological change is going to serve people rather than people being oppressed by technological change.
April 16, 1984

Briefly let me say that the inadequacy of the Government's approach to technological change is visible in communities. It is visible by virtue of the fact that there are so many unemployed people today. The Government gives no evidence of introducing strategies that will be adequate to provide employment for Canadians. We know from experience that the Government's approach to technological change does not measure up. It is really totally inadequate.
The Conservatives have rightly introduced a motion today calling our attention to training to meet technological change, but the problem with the Conservative approach to technological change is that you have to ask the question, training for what? If you are going to train, you have to plan jobs. When you are hidebound by a free enterprise ideology and you simply leave economic development to the marketplace alone, then, Mr. Speaker, you are likely to end up with a situation no different from the situation from which we are suffering today, namely record high unemployment. I must remind my Tory colleagues that it is not only important to train people for work, but we have to plan the economy in such a way that we will provide work for all Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to congratulate the Hon. Member for bringing out the issue of notification of the introduction of new technology. Common sense tells us that in Canada today technology has been introduced into the workplace very, very successfully when there has been sufficient advance notification and when there has been a good collective bargaining process in place. I wanted to get to that, but I ran out of time and I thank the Hon. Member for bringing that issue forward.
However, the Hon. Member concludes his speech with the question "training for what?" I suggest to him that if he had spent the last six months, as I have, trying to look at the literature, meeting with representatives of industry, business and provincial governments, he would find that you are forced, in a common-sense way, to come to the conclusion that we do not know what the jobs of the future will be. We do know that we will not have them unless we are competitive and unless we have broad education which gives people sufficient background skills to be inventive so that they can bring forward the new products and services that will employ people.
In that context, I wonder why the New Democratic Party remains attached to the shorter work week. In nations where the shorter work week has been tried it is not producing the jobs that theory said it would. And I wonder why the New Democratic Party is still attached to the levy-grant system, Mr. Speaker. Surely the levy-grant system is a system dedicated to the promotion of the status quo, that is, the training of people for jobs which are most likely to become obsolete. That is the experience of other nations with regard to the levy-grant system, and that is the experience with the shorter work week. Could the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-St. James (Mr. Supply
Keeper) indicate to us whether or not the NDP supports the concept of broader educational patterns, things like computer literacy, not because we know what the jobs are going to be but simply because we know the computers are going to be involved in them? Therefore, a broader educational picture, a total societal commitment to more education for everybody, is better than a shorter work week and better than a levy-grant system.

subtopic: BUSINESS OF SUPPLY ALLOTTED DAY S O. 62-TECHNOLOGICAL CHANGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is clear and obvious that we have to have a very broad educational base for all Canadians if we are going to have people with the skills and abilities to operate in a technological society. That is a given. We have to have very broad-based educational programs. As a part of that we have to move governments to deal with the whole question of functional illiteracy. We have to have broad-based education so that people are functionally literate. We have to deal with the presently existing career problem of functional illiteracy. We have long been urging the Government to attack functional illiteracy.
With regard to the question of the shorter work week, it is a concrete, important step toward sharing the work in society and toward sharing income in society. Obviously it cannot be the only thing; it has to be part of the over-all package. It has to be part of an over-all strategy the aim of which is the provision of employment for all Canadians. I am surprised that my Tory colleague has rejected the notion of a shorter work week. As long as we bring in new technology, as long as we increase productivity, why can people not look forward to a share in that wealth? Why can they not look forward to more adequate holidays? Why can they not look forward to early retirement? Why can they not look forward to a more decent work week? I think the shorter work week is an essential element of a full employment strategy. We should not be operating simply on the basis of growth for growth's sake; we have to use economic growth to serve people.
With regard to the levy-grant system, this is a system which would be set in place in order to encourage training in industry by industry.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in his remarks the Hon. Member said that we could not dare trust the marketplace to determine what kind of jobs our young people and those who need retraining will have in the future. Whom would he like us to trust? Would he like us to trust the civil servants, the bureaucrats or politicians? Does he suggest that perhaps the New Democratic Party would be better to be trusted in terms of job creation and opportunities for young people? Is his idea that somewhere along the way the state, in its all-seeing wisdom, can create jobs and know where those jobs are going to be in a technological world? Is there some other place where we can look for expertise, other than the demands there will be for new products and so on? My son has a business today that two years ago did not exist anywhere in North America. We would not have that kind of development in his new world.

subtopic: BUSINESS OF SUPPLY ALLOTTED DAY S O. 62-TECHNOLOGICAL CHANGE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this is a typical Tory question which tends to distort rather than inform. It is not a matter of the market place or not the marketplace but a matter of planning in order to be effective in the world market. Individual firms plan. They have a strategic notion of where they are going. Likewise, it is important for a nation to plan where it is going. You cannot get to a particular destination unless you chart your way. What is missing in the Canadian economy is the laying out of a plan in order to indicate how we are going to achieve employment for all Canadians. How are we going to achieve the necessary economic growth that can put people back to work? It is not enough to leave it to the results of the marketplace without planning. We have to combine planning with the marketplace.

subtopic: BUSINESS OF SUPPLY ALLOTTED DAY S O. 62-TECHNOLOGICAL CHANGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, following on the theme of who plans, I have here an article in The Globe and Mail of May 7, 1983, almost a year ago. There is quote after quote about Liberal federal Government planning regarding priority occupations, yet when people graduate with particular sets of skills there are no jobs. In the meantime, there are jobs but people with no skills. We have had decade after decade of central planning for training for occupations of the future.
I have one simple question. Is the Hon. Member willing to redefine the concept of work to include the concept of school and retraining? If he is willing to do that, does he hold to the position that the work week should be reduced? Does he believe that people should be engaged in productive activity, including school, fewer than 35 to 40 hours per week, or is he willing to redefine work so that a larger portion of a person's life cycle is spent in being retrained, re-educated and further educated?

subtopic: BUSINESS OF SUPPLY ALLOTTED DAY S O. 62-TECHNOLOGICAL CHANGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, obviously it is necessary for people to spend an increasing portion of their life in training and education. We need more flexible systems in order that people can get the training they need. This is not contradictory to the notion of a shorter work week; it is complementary to a
shorter work week. If people can get the kind of training they need, obviously when they are training, others can do the job they would otherwise have to continue doing. The notion of paid educational leave would have a positive impact with regard to employment because when an individual recognized his right to train, someone else would have to be brought in to do the job. That would provide employment for more people.
The Hon. Member also talked about planning. He said that we had central planning and it did not get us any place. Planning does not have to be central planning. There are some decisions that have to be made centrally, but a lot more decisions have to be made locally. It depends on the framework and structure put in place to ensure that the planning is done in an intelligent way. Just because the Liberals have botched up planning is no reason to throw out the notion of planning. If we want our economy to serve people, we have to plan how it can be done.

Mr. Speaker, I am surprised that the Liberals are not participating in this debate today. May I preface my remarks by congratulating my colleague from CalgaryWest (Mr. Hawkes), not only for bringing forward this very timely motion but also to congratulate him together with a colleague in the other place, Senator Nurgitz, on the release of an excellent report by the task force on technological change in manpower training. It is a Progressive Conservative Party report, I might point out. It is an excellent report with some excellent recommendations. The Government has been asking for some positive recommendations from our Party and has been receiving them. The last two have been on Revenue Canada and on manpower training. I hope the Government will take them to heart because they are well thought out, well researched, well reasoned and will work.
I want to go back into the history of training in our country and what has gone on in the past that leads us to where we are today. For far too long we in this country have been importing our skilled labour, primarily from Europe. It has been extremely easy for companies to get skilled people from Europe because of the training programs there. I say to my colleague from the NDP that it is not because of the grant-levy system. The apprenticeship program in Europe goes back many hundreds of years. Apprentices are guaranteed to complete their apprenticeship. That is the difference between European apprenticeships and those in our country today. In this country we use the last on first off principle. An apprentice starts his apprenticeship with a Canadian company not knowing for sure whether he will finish it or not. That is a major problem here which is not experienced in the European picture.
When a young apprentice in Europe applies, is accepted and starts the long journey to getting his journeyman's papers, he is assured that he will in fact complete his apprenticeship. A
April 16, 1984

job is not guaranteed with that company once he receives his journeyman's papers, but he does receive his apprenticeship.
I am told that in the manufacturing industry the first year of an apprenticeship costs a company some $60,000, what with the training, salary and loss of productivity within the plant for that period of time. That is a tremendous amount of money. When you look at something like that, you understand why companies go to Europe to import skilled labour. For $60,000 they can do a tremendous amount of looking in Europe for the skills required and pay the moving expenses of an individual or family to take a skilled labour job in Canada.
It is interesting to note that in this country training has primarily been undertaken by the small and medium-sized manufacturing firms as opposed to the large industries. For example, much to my surprise General Motors began an apprenticeship program within the last three or four years and has now set up quite a fine school in its Windsor plant. This was the first time that had been done.
When we were travelling around looking into the unemployment problem, officials of General Motors readily admitted to us that they had stolen all of their skilled labourers from small and medium-sized firms. In other words, they had let the small and medium-sized firms do the training and they took the expertise. That situation is changing slowly. Companies are beginning to realize that they do in fact have a responsibility to train employees and that it is very important to their increased productivity and competitiveness that they must in fact begin to train employees right here at home.
Another problem is that the skilled labour market in Europe has almost dried up. The remuneration and fringe benefits offered to skilled labourers in Europe do not motivate those labourers to come to a new country. The drop in emigration of skilled labourers has also forced companies in Canada to begin their own training programs and these programs must continue.
While I am on this subject, I would like to speak about the grant-levy system. Variations on this system can be found in Europe. France has a system which is entirely different from that in Britain but it is still called the grant-levy system. The theory of this system is that all of the manufacturing companies in one particular field pay into a fund, those who receive training can withdraw money from this fund to pay for the training and those who do not receive training simply pay money in without receiving any back. When we examined this program, we found that the grant-levy system was in fact not working and that it created a huge bureaucray. I can understand why members of the New Democratic Party like this system. It creates another huge bureaucracy and they love that kind of thing. That is their idea of job creation.
The policing that must go on within this system is phenomenal. People enter individual plants every week to make sure that training is occurring and that the proper forms are being filled out, et cetera. The people who participate in this system are so frustrated with the bureaucracy that they simply do not
Supply
see it working. Others are happy simply to pay into the fund without receiving training because in the long run it saves them problems and the hassles of bureaucracy. Once a year they simply pay into the fund. I do not think that that is really the answer to the problem we are experiencing in Canada.
Another problem with the grant-levy system is that so many companies are exempt from it. Employers with fewer than 10 employees, those with their own programs and many other employers are exempt. It is a bureaucratic nightmare. If Canadian businesses are saying anything to the Government, they are telling the Government to stay out of their hair or whatever little of it they have left. I can see that the Hon. Member for Sarnia-Lambton (Mr. Cullen) is winding up to make a comment so I thought I would say that before he did, Mr. Speaker.
The grant-levy system has not proven to be the answer. It simply does not work. When it does operate, it creates an enormous bureaucracy. We visited the operation in Britain and found the administration of the system required its own building. There were regulations like we have never seen before. It was a very interesting trip. I am sure that if the Government looked into that program in any detail, it would find that the grant-levy system simply does not work.
I would like to speak for a moment about one of the findings of the task force which has been reported from time to time and that is the high percentage of people in the country who are functionally illiterate. When I was involved in the task force on employment opprtunities in the 1980s, one of the greatest shocks I received as a member of that task force was to learn of the high percentage of people who are functionally illiterate. I think all of us from all Parties who were members of that task force were very surprised by this. Unfortunately, when this finding was included in a report, the provincial governments and teachers' associations interpreted it as an attack on their ability to teach in the public school systems. However, it was not that at all.
There are many people in the country who, for one reason or another, leave school at a very early age. Perhaps they leave school to work with their parents in the fishing industry or the hunting and trapping industry. There are many new Canadians who have not experienced the luxury of an educational system such as the one in Canada and who find it very difficult to read and write in either one of the Canada's official languages, or in their own language for that matter, because they have not had the opportunity to do so. We desperately need an attack on this problem. At one time the federal Government had a national reading program and was very concerned with the problem, but lately it seems that the Government is not paying too much attention to the illiteracy problem in the country.
I am finding that there are many Outreach groups in communities across this great land of ours which are very interested in getting involved and helping the illiterate. It is sometimes difficult to identify those who are illiterate but the staff at local Canadian employment offices will admit that they can readily identify those who have trouble reading or

April 16, 1984
Supply
filling out forms and who need help. Before we can teach people the skills that are required for the times ahead, we must address the problem of illiteracy.
We read every day about the drop in the numbers of children who are attending school, about teachers who are being laid off and about schools which are being closed down. I know that schools have been closed down in the riding of the Hon. Member for Niagara Falls (Mr. MacBain). I believe we can use these facilities, not only as training areas for tackling this problem but also as daycare centres which will take care of children so that people can upgrade their skills. The challenge exists and I will return to that challenge in a moment.
I would like to speak about native people for a moment. Aboriginal people in the country are experiencing job discrimination; there is no question about that. The aboriginal groups are a great source of skilled labour. Native people must be given the opportunity to be trained and to receive the education that is available to the rest of Canadian society. I would hope that any national training program would pay special attention to the aboriginal people of the country who are experiencing the highest unemployment rate in the country.
When speaking about the unemployment rate, the 11.3 per cent or 11.4 per cent of the population who are unemployed today, one of the interesting things about that figure is that it does not include native people. If they were included, the figure would be much higher. Through any training program, aboriginal people must be given the opportunity to develop the skills that others have the opportunity of developing.
I would like to deal with co-operation for a moment. Because of the Constitution, education is the responsibility of the provincial governments. They guard that responsibility jealously. I cannot blame them; I understand. But when we are talking about training for skills which will be required in the foreseeable future and when we are talking about mobility of labour from one province to another, from one region to another, we must talk about co-operation.
I think twice a year the Council of Education Ministers gets together. There is very little federal involvement in that organization. When it comes to national training, the federal Government must participate more in a co-operative manner with that Council. There is a great necessity to involve labour and industry in meaningful discussions on manpower training. I have visited company after company in my riding and I am concerned when I see skilled workers becoming older and there are no younger ones to take their place. In a very short period of time the manufacturers will be coming to us and saying that they do not have any skilled labour and that they will have to go to England, Germany of France to find it. It is important that all levels of government sit down together and seriously discuss our training objectives and our training programs.
After travelling from the rocky shores of Newfoundland to Victoria, to the Northwest Territories and all places in between, visiting union halls, manufacturing plants, small businesses and high-tech industries, I realize that we have a
fabulous opportunity in Canada to be a leader in many areas of industry in the world. We must remain competitive and to do that we must become more productive. To achieve those goals we must have better training in the country.
Canada has the greatest opportunity of any country in the world. I do not think any Member of the House would disagree with that. Anyone who has travelled around the world is happy to come back home. We must stop bickering and his combativeness which seems to have developed and reached a crisis porportion today. We must start co-operating and ensuring that training programs and the expertise of the nation are allowed to grow and to flourish.

speechtext:
Since the beginning of the debate, Mr. Speaker, the Progressive Conservatives have created the impression that they are quite proud of the motion before the House. If, as they claim, the problem is that serious and if they have so much to say about it, how is it that their motion does not call for a vote? Just what do they have to say about the situation described in the motion? In any event, they may talk all day long about what they see as a crucial issue- they talk about their own future Government! They should not dream in colour nor count their chickens before they are hatched. With respect to new technology, or the rapid technological change, as the motion puts it, this will give us an opportunity today to consider what the Government has been doing these past few years, particularly since the adoption of the 1982 National Training Act which has paved the way for a new national program. Obviously, if Canadian workers want to have the highly paid future jobs, they will have to develop the skills required by industries in leading sectors, and this motion gives me an opportunity today to say what we have been doing. Mr. Speaker, we do not want to take a short-sighted approach, and that is why the Government was prompted by the worldwide economic crisis to provide Canadians with the National Training Program to make it a lot easier for our labour force to adapt itself to the new conditions of the labour market. The National Training Program is an offshoot of the National Training Act adopted by the House a little over two years ago. Having weighed the pros and cons of this program, Hon. Members-particularly our colleagues opposite-know full well that the Government did not spare any effort to improve vocational training and reassess its purposes. Our progress in that field stem from the National Training Program. Basically, Mr. Speaker, the Government had two objectives when it introduced the National Training Act in the House. I should like to mention them so that our Progressive Conservative colleagues will be able to refresh their memory and see for themselves just what has been done in answer to their motion of today. The first objective of the National Training Act was to create a pool of skilled workers needed by employers anxious to expand their operations. There cannot be any doubt about it, the future of our industries is at stake. The second objective, a sequel to the first one, is to help Canadian men and women become more competitive and more productive on the labour market. It stands to reason that the future of all Canadians is at stake. Those are the two objectives of the National Training Act, and discussions have already been held with the provinces, labour and management. In that respect, the Official Opposition Party has been doing a lot of talking and came out with its famous report at Mont-Sainte-Marie. The Minister himself referred to it in answer to a question in the House, explaining what the Canadian Government had done precisely to come to grips with new technology. The

April 16, 1984
Supply
Liberal Government considers new technology as something important, and that is why we have been trying to attract high technology industries in every province throughout Canada. Bell Helicopter immediately comes to mind, Mr. Speaker, and I can still recall that Members of the Official Opposition had scoffed at that suggestion. They were saying that perhaps it should not locate in Quebec, or even wondering why it should even consider Quebec in the first place. I do remember some of their questions! Well, Mr. Speaker, the Canadian Government thought in terms of high technology precisely because it wants to emphasize programs and industries such as Bell Helicopter.
In order to achieve the purpose of the National Training Act, the government of Canada has established a manpower training strategy the implementation of which is continuing under the act.
If I may, Mr. Speaker, I should like briefly to describe the key elements of the employment opportunity strategy which the government has elaborated for the 80s.
First of all, it is absolutely necessary to secure the best possible information available on job requirements. It is clear that if we lack this basic information in the area of advanced technology and do not know in what direction we should go, we are doomed from the start. In my opinion, it is of the utmost importance to know where we are going. To this end, the government is working in cooperation with business and labour to ward the establishment of the Canadian Occupational Projection System. Also, Mr. Speaker, it was equally necessary to amend our institutional training scheme to ensure the success of our initiatives. Training schools must adapt to the new conditions prevailing on the labour market to provide workers with useful skills.
Such an adaptation is difficult because the number of trainees is not increasing. Special funds, therefore, had to be allocated to up-date training facilities wherever necessary. Projects financed by the Skills Growth Fund under the National Training Act are starting to yield very concrete results of which we can be very proud, Mr. Speaker.
In this connection, Mr. Speaker, when we consider the use which is being made by our teaching institutions, such as the Quebec CEGEPs and similar institutions in other provinces, as far as grades are concerned . . . Recently, the minister had also announced allocations to the Skills Growth Fund in Ontario, in Quebec and throughout Canada. A number of Quebec CEGEPs have received as much as $8 and $10 million, both in Montreal and the surrounding area where there are advanced technology industries requiring workers which highly specialized skills. That is what we have done through the Skills Growth Fund, and that is why we have made funds available to it and they are available because the National Training Act has been passed.
I believe that, by falling in with the requests from these financial institutions, the Canadian Government is also
answering the aspirations of businessmen and organized labour, who are well aware that, if we want to have high technology industries, keep those we have or attract new ones, we must have the skilled workers they call for. This is what we are doing through the National Training Act and the Skills Growth Fund.
The Government is constantly seeking to improve the amount and the quality of the training that is required by the industry. In particular, we must increase on-the-job training in the occupational fields essential for economic growth in Canada. The new programs for general industrial training and training in occupational areas where specialized manpower is in short supply are essential tools for bringing about the required improvements.
Other initiatives are needed, Mr. Speaker, to better integrate training programs within the institutions and the industries. We are working on it in co-operation with the Provinces, the employers, the unions and our specialists in the Department of Employment and Immigration.
In a fast changing world, workers will have to go on acquiring new skills throughout their career. Consequently, we shall have to find ways of allowing them the time to do so. Work sharing and development leave will have to be used increasingly for this purpose during the upcoming decade.
Mr. Speaker, the Canadian Government does not specialize in the closing down of plants as a means of solving the problems related to the upheaval that has been witnessed on the labour market in recent years. However, the Government is aware that we are entering an age where outdated industries will have either to modernize or be replaced by others better suited to the new labour market conditions.
Sure enough, this adaptation is hard to achieve in certain areas of the country where it is sometimes suggested that businesses are closing down. Mr. Speaker, we want to work at bringing in new industries and to offer retraining programs for these workers who, very often, do not have very many years of schooling and have been working for several years for companies which are closing down because of various problems. Naturally, it is not always easy. However, we have developed programs in certain sectors designed to help people who had to retrain or had to quit their jobs.
Of course, we must help industry which choose the lofty road to progress, and we must also provide special assistance to the workers of industries on the downgrade. Some businesses in high technology industries must get more generous assistance, because even though their order books might not yet be full, this government favours technological progress and must be willing to make the required efforts to prevent the industries with a future from sinking.
April 16, 1984

Mr. Speaker, we believe there are two factors that have a major importance when determining the impact of technological changes, namely those sectors in our economy which will be the most affected by these changes and the speed with which these changes materialize. In working out this concept in co-operation with the other Government levels, as well as with business and labour, the primary aim of the federal Government was to set up an early warning mechanism. Mr. Speaker, this mechanism is the Canadian Occupational Projections System.
As we have emphasized several times, flexibility is the key of success for the National Training Act, and I mean its flexibility to adapt to the ups and downs of the economy and the requirements of the labour market. The basic component of this flexibility is the Canadian Occupational Projections System.
With the information provided by industry, the unions, the Provinces and the federal Government, the Canadian Occupational Projections System, gets specific data on the trends in the labour market. Thanks to this system, fields of occupation \ which should have priority can be identified and the training grants provided by the Government can be directed to the appropriate disciplines. In other words, Mr. Speaker, we subsidize occupational training wherever it is genuinely needed.
Mr. Speaker, the substantial amounts available for occupational training in Canada shows the intent of the Government to guarantee that Canadian workers can meet the challenges of the upcoming decade. We still believe that the mainspring of the economy is the private sector, supported by practical and necessary initiatives taken by the Government. The economic interdependence of the industrialized and developing countries is a factor which we must more and more take into account in our projections because Canada has to be able to keep its rank as one of the most industrialized countries.
Mr. Speaker, let me now deal with one of the most important programs designed to help businesses face the challenge of new technology. I am speaking about the National Industrial Training Program, which is twofold. First, there is the general industrial training aimed at avoiding shortages of qualified workers, preventing lay-offs due to technological changes and promoting the training of specific groups within the industry. As an example, I could mention the programs for training women in non-traditional occupations, and those which provide training in skills where there is a shortage of specialized workers and which are aimed at promoting training in highly specialized fields of occupation, reducing chronic shortages in such fields of occupation and bringing the employers to enhance the skills of their own workers instead of recruiting foreign workers.
Under this National Industrial Training Program, the employer may be eligible for wage grants covering up to 100 per cent of the instructor's fees, up to 100 per cent of the costs of training aids, up to 75 per cent of registration fees for
Supply
courses when training is provided by a public or private institution, up to 75 per cent of special general travelling and living expenses incurred by workers in training, and up to 75 per cent of the costs of course preparation.
During one year, Mr. Speaker, the employer is paid 50 per cent of the trainee's wages. This refund may even be more generous in the case of certain types of workers, such as the physically handicapped. Canadian employers are eligible for close to $95 million under this program in 1984-85.
In many respects, Mr. Speaker, our educational systems do not always make it possible for Canadian men and women to develop the skills required on the labour market. It does represent a serious problem because the Canadian economy is bound to stagnate unless people can indeed acquire appropriate professional skills. The National Industrial Training Program is the federal Government's major mechanism to enable Canadian men and women to acquire those new skills for which demand is very strong.
In 1984-85, Mr. Speaker-and this is in answer to those who censure the Government for remaining idle and failing to cooperate with a view to providing Canadian workers with adequate technological training-the federal Government will spend in excess of $902 million for the institutional training of more than 220,000 future workers. This program is more specifically aimed at young school drop-outs, women, native people and others who are at a disadvantage when it comes to employment. Here again, people will be trained in skills for which there will be a strong demand when their apprenticeship is completed.
Mr. Speaker, I would suggest that Canadians are aware that there are no simplistic solutions to the current need for new jobs, nor ready-made answers to the challenges of tomorrow's labour market. We do expect very positive results from our strategy to train people for immediate openings and to expand the labour market for the future. The efforts of the Canadian Government reflect the underlying principle to which we fully subscribe: job creation is first and foremost the private sector's responsibility. The role of the Government is to create the proper climate or environment to help Canadian workers and make it easier for them to face the challenges of the labour market. It is our duty as elected representatives to propose new structures to ensure the smooth operation of the labour market. I think we should also thank our colleagues opposite for their efforts to make the Canadian people aware of the situation, while at the same time reminding them that programs such as those I just mentioned and under which $902 million have been set aside for institutional training in 1984-85 are a giant step in the right direction.
As I said a few moments ago, Mr. Speaker, I think that this motion sets the high technology challenge in its proper perspective. Even before the Conservative Party set up their famous task force which made headlines last week, the Canadian Government had already established the foundation

April 16, 1984

required by the National Training Act which was adopted by the House two years ago and which just happens to be the answer to the need for more skilled workers and assistance programs geared to future progress.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member refers to stock Liberal answers. I say to him that we have been putting up in this House with stock progressive conservative questions for 20 years. They are always against something. Very seldom are they in support of anything. What they have been in support of on occasion, when they put forward a motion, is the death penalty for instance, but otherwise they are always against.
And when he suggests that in his mind his proposal addresses the issue of people's plight, I cannot agree with him because, in view of the various programs we have in place, he only has to look at the restructured programs, what, with job

April 16, 1984

creation and help provisions we have brought forward. If I refer specifically to his question and the motion, one has only to look at programs such as CAREER ACCESS for the young, CAREER ACCESS for people discriminated against under current employment conditions, because those people can go to the Canada Employment centres. Employers receive grants, not only under the Training Act but under our Job Creation Programs, to help face the lack of employment. It is a pleasure to be able to speak on this motion today, Mr. Speaker. I notice that in the traditional style of Opposition motions it is framed in a condemnatory way. I do not think it is the intention to be condemnatory this afternoon, although we might point out some of the shortcomings and failing of the Government. Rather, the idea is to encourage debate on a most important subject, and hopefully some good ideas will come out of it.
I would like to read briefly part of the motion that we are discussing. The emphasis is "to provide adequate training and retraining opportunities that would enable Canadian workers to feel confident"-and I emphasize "to feel confident"- "about their ability to deal with the challenges of rapid technological change". It is not by accident that the motion uses those words. They express the idea of Canadians having confidence in their own ability to deal with changes that are in the process of occurring and will change in the future.
We on this side, unlike our socialist friends to the left, do not think it is the state that should be there to provide every last person in Canada with a job. I do not think that is a reasonable goal. What we can do as a national Government is provide the background and the framework in which Canadians can be confident in their ability to find work and to find meaningful and socially useful things to do. At present that confidence does not exist in Canada. If you travel around the

April 16, 1984
Supply
country, you will find that there is fear of the future, sometimes the very near future, as to what might happen. People know how difficult it is for them to be able to make the necessary changes.
In order to illustrate the way I think we should go as a nation, I shall retell a story which I read in a book in the Parliamentary Library when I was reading about Greek history and philosophy. It is one of my favourite subjects and I think I share that in common with another well known Member of this House. This was a story of a person who eventually became a very famous philosopher and teacher; I am sorry to say I have forgotten his name. However, when he was a young man, less than 20 years of age, he was shipwrecked somewhere in the Aegean Sea. He managed to make it to shore. When he arrived on shore in a state of near exhaustion, he had no money and no clothing on his back. He arrived there destitute. He had no friends. He really had nothing going for himself. After a period of months and years he was able not only to survive but to earn the esteem of the people where he lived. He became quite wealthy and well respected. Finally he found his way back into the mainstream of Greek life.
As a result of that experience in his further teaching down the road he stressed the point that his parents had wanted him to enjoy and to participate in life. Although he had nothing when he arrived on this island after being shipwrecked he was able to make a living, he was able to do something useful and he was able to be part of the mainsteam of existence.
I think that is the attitude we should have in teaching in Canada. We should not have to concentrate on finding a job for everybody, but we should make sure that whatever happens to people they will be confident and have the ability to make the best go of it themselves. Things like money, possessions and social status come and go. They are ephemeral. Ability, training and skill beget confidence and they last forever. That is the way we should go, Mr. Speaker.
There are now, as we can ascertain, changes in society and we expect these changes will continue. These changes are not only occurring in Canada but right across the developed world. They are no secret to us. Let me outline some of the changes that are taking place in society. I made a brief list. It is expected that people during the course of a lifetime will not have one specific job. A person will not be a mechanic in a certain factory and spend all of his or her working life doing one job at one location. A person will have several jobs throughout a lifetime. I will come back to this a little later.
There will also have to be flexibility in location. I am thinking specifically of the situation in Ottawa. It is pretty difficult to find anyone who admits to having been born in Ottawa. Most people come from somewhere else other than Ottawa. Many people do not expect to stay here for the rest of their lives. They look upon being in Ottawa as a period before moving on to bigger and better things elsewhere. In this day and age when you can leave Ottawa in the morning and within 24 hours be in Adelaide, Australia, it is something we can expect and it is something we will have to learn to live with. I
do not take the parochial view which seems to be common in many areas of the land. I do not even take a national view. I see people travelling throughout the world in order to take the best advantages wherever they might occur.
Another point already mentioned is that education will have to be ongoing. A person will not leave school at 16, 20, or whatever, and consider that the end of his or her education. Education will continue on.
I see that the Steward is about to take the Mace from the Table. Perhaps we can call it one o'clock and I shall be here again at two o'clock, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, 1984 is the year of the unemployed. In the riding of Erie alone, close to 600 jobs were lost in the past month. Our Government is having a great deal of difficulty coming to terms with this problem. It is throwing money around like there is no tomorrow, and yet it seems unable to adapt our economy to build a basis for future prosperity in a rapidly changing and competitive world.
Our problem, simply stated, is that our resource base, traditionally our strong point, has been eroded by foreign competition. For instance, our share of world nickel production has dropped from 80 per cent to 35 per cent during the 1970s. In the same period our share of world copper production has dropped by nearly a quarter. Our share of the world market for lumber has dropped from 50 per cent in 1970 to 40 per cent. A similar trend is seen in the manufacturing sector. Canada's share of the world's manufactured exports has dropped by more than a third, from 4.8 per cent in 1970, to 3 per cent in 1980. We seem to be exporting less and importing
more. In 1970 imports accounted for 25 per cent of consumer purchases. The figure is now 32 per cent.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday, April 15, marked the traditional opening day for commercial salmon fishing on the West Coast for all gears and in all areas. This year only the west coast of Vancouver Island was opened on April 15, and then only for troller men. Stocks are sadly depleted, and no Canada-U.S. agreement is in place to preserve what is left and share it equitably.
The West Coast fishery is not just in "Desperate Straits"; it is in "Crisis Passage, Depletion Sound", and "Gravity Gulf'.

Millions of dollars are tied up on the West Coast in commercial fishing boats, sportscraft, fishing gear, and in back-up industries such as marinas, gear manufacturers, boat builders, and supply services in both the commercial and the sports fishery. Uncertainty about future prospects is causing increasing concern throughout the industry. The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Hawkes:
That this House condemns the Government for its failure to work co-operatively with the provinces, business, labour, voluntary organizations and the educational community to provide adequate training and retraining opportunities that would enable Canadian workers to feel confident about their ability to deal with the challenges of rapid technological change.

Mr. Speaker, when I was interrupted by the luncheon break I was in the middle of discussing certain social changes that were taking place in the Field of employment. The fourth point that I have listed, Mr. Speaker, is that in the future people will have to be more self-reliant. They will Find that they will not be able to rely upon a single employer for employment security throughout their lifetime, nor will they be able to rely on governments. People who put their trust in governments generally end up falling flat on their faces at some point in time. They will have to become more self-reliant as time goes on. Our education will have to reflect that.
Another change that will occur in the future, and which has to a certain extent occurred already, is that people will not rely on one single speciFic job for a source of income. Presently most people in Canada have a principal source of income from a job and very little income from other sources. Maybe in the future, as the number of hours per week consumed by working at a speciFic job decreases, you will Find that people will have other things to do. It is quite conceivable that they might work in the standard, accepted sense and do other things which will bring in additional revenue. It may be a second job in an entirely different Field in which they have a great deal of personal interest. It could be investment income because

April 16, 1984
Supply
people will have time to do other things for themselves. It could be income from entrepreneurial activity of one kind or another, or from property ownership.
I have noticed that in certain professions this is going on today. Not too long ago I sat on the flight deck of a Hercules aircraft and spoke to the flight crew. Most of them worked a couple of weeks a month. They could only fly so many hours and after that they went back to their home bases. Most of them were involved in other things. They were involved in voluntary organizations as well as profit-making activities. I think that is a good trend to see. In the future people will not be tied to working 40 or 50 hours a week for one employer; they will have a series of sources of income.
This will blur the distinction that our socialist friends are at pains to keep. If people operate in the way that I have suggested, there will not be that clear distinction between what the NDP call the working class, the capital owning class, and other types. Everyone will be involved as wage earners, investors and entrepreneurs. The politics of the day will have to reflect this. It is happening today. We see support for the socialist party represented here waning day by day.
The developments that I have outlined appear to me to be exiciting developments. The Government should act in consort with these trends and not try to go out of its way to oppose them, as presently appears to be the case on occasion.
We still have very parochial thinking, particularly at the provincial level in certain provinces. I have been a party to this myself, but I think that on the whole we should take a Canada-wide or even an international view of matters rather than being restrictive in our thinking in terms of a single province or part thereof.
Again with respect to education, there is still a tendency on the part of government to look upon education as something that takes place between the ages of five and 20, or whenever one leaves university. The Government has not yet accepted the notion of education as being something that is ongoing and a process that will last a lifetime.
The Government is still very much involved with hand-out programs. It has not got around to addressing problems on a long-term basis. It considers that our current difficulties will go away and it simply throws a few dollars here and there into one of its various alphabet soup programs. It is not really addressing the long-term problems and long-term societal changes.
For these reasons I would like to congratulate the Hon. Member for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes) on the task force report on technological change and manpower retraining, of which he was the prime mover. It is a subject to which he has given a great deal of thought, both presently with this report and also with other members of the parliamentary task force on the same subject.
Many of the ideas contained herein are not really new, revolutionary ideas, but the task force has collected and collated a wide variety of views from Canadians in all walks of life and has effectively crystallized these ideas out of the vagueness that existed before. It is a distillation of thought and an arrangement thereof in logical order. I am sure that in the future we will look back at this report and it will serve as a blueprint of what governments might do in the field of technological change and manpower retraining.
I do not propose to have all of the solutions to some of the problems I have raised, but I have a few which I would like to deal with later. In the next couple of minutes I would like to point out some personal observations about where we seem to be going at the present time. I have three illustrations.
The first deals with the manpower offices as they exist in my constituency. Some 15 years ago we did not have any at all and things seemed to be going reasonably well. There were not high rates of unemployment and maybe we did not need them. It is hard to judge which came first, the chicken or the egg, so to speak. However, there were no manpower offices or anything of that nature 15 years ago. Today, they must be staffed with a complement of somewhere between 50 and 100 people, when one considers the Territories as a whole. The problem has not been alleviated. If anything, the problem that did not exist when we had no manpower offices has now become a very difficult problem with which to deal. I am not so sure that the hiring of 50 to 100 people, the provision of office space and all the money that is spent on these things might be the best use of resources, human, financial and otherwise, available to the Government.
Another illustration is the difficulty people face if they want to give employment, particularly to summer students. I know that it used to be my practice some years ago to hire one or two summer students. Now, the roadblocks that are put in someone's place are almost insurmountable. I would not consider doing this today because I know full well what would happen. For the next five years I would be getting reports from Statistics Canada threatening to throw me in jail unless I filled them in. There are problems with the tax people and unemployment insurance people. There are all manner of problems and roadblocks which prevent small employers from hiring people, especially on a temporary basis. That is unfortunate because surely part of the training of young people, apart from schooling proper, is to get experience in work situations, particularly during the summer recess. It makes it very difficult and is unfortunate for the student when the Government erects all of these roadblocks.
You are signalling that my time is almost up, Mr. Speaker. I have several pages to go and I will not be able to get to my solutions. I like giving the solutions better than stating the problems. However, the last illustration is that of a silly make-work scheme. Last summer I travelled throughout my riding in which there were Summer Canada Works programs into which the Government throws quite a few thousand dollars. In two locations I noticed that there were unused fields in the middle of towns. They were about 15 acres each. Students were out there with little sticks with six-inch blades on them, cutting the grass or mowing the hay on these waste
April 16, 1984

areas. It was a scheme to employ perhaps a dozen young people for a period of six weeks. One man with a scythe could1 have done it all in one week and one person operating a power mower could have done it in one day. It represents a complete waste of government time and money and a waste of the talents of young people.
I believe my time has expired. It is unfortunate that you could not have heard all of my great solutions, Mr. Speaker. Perhaps I will be able to give them to you on another occasion.
