Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate with my colleagues in the debate on an issue which, to my mind, is basic, especially after travelling throughout Canada and meeting with employ-1 ers, union members, voluntary organizations and young people, and then considering today the motion moved by the Progressive Conservative Party to single out our failure to work together with the provinces, business and labour organizations.
Mr. Speaker, it would seem that our colleagues do not work in the same country as we do, but there is indeed one undeniable fact: I am just back from a trip across Canada during which I visited the ten provinces and the Northwest Territories. The Hon. Member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson) should make an effort to recall that I was in Yellowknife about three weeks ago to attend the Arctic Games and at the same time to meet with employers, union leaders and all those who are involved in youth employment, as far as I am directly concerned, and to discuss the employment situation in Canada generally.
I am here today, Mr. Speaker, to speak on my own behalf since I happen to be Minister of State for Youth, and on behalf of my colleague the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Roberts) who is now in Montreal to sign an agreement with a group called "EPOC" with which I met a few years ago and which is working with a group of Montreal businessmen to train young people and find employment for young drop-outs who are experiencing difficulties because they have been unemployed for several years or thrown out of the labour market as a result of their running afoul of the law, which does not make it any easier for them to land a job. Earlier today, the Minister signed an agreement with that dynamic group that, in nine cases out of ten, has been able to find employment for young people who have been rehabilitated over the past ten years through federal Government sponsored programs.
Today, I think we have not learned much from the report of the task force of our Progressive Conservative colleagues who said:

The task force reports that Canadian industry is slow to recognize much of the potential of merging technologies.

As if we were in 1940, Mr. Speaker.
[English\
The task force terms a disgrace the fact that the public educational institutions are often unable to afford needed equipment for training and hence make appropriate changes in curricula to reflect changing skill needs.

There again, Mr. Speaker, I think that, even after voting on the estimates and the expenditure items approved by this House, the Opposition Members do not even realize that we have a Skills Growth Fund worth several million dollars. I would at least ask them to read the official document.
On the other hand, Mr. Speaker, in my tour of Canada and as the Members opposite have pointed out in their report, I noticed that the labour market has been undergoing a major transformation because of high technology, silicone chips, robotics, and so on. Of course, when we see challenger's Canadarm, we realize that Canada is involved in the progress of technology and that all our young people and our working men and women in Canada are anxious to play a role in the many new jobs created in the high technology areas.

Most of us have already felt the impact of the new revolution in one way or another. One has only to look at the proliferation of home computers, automated bank tellers and home video equipment to realize how quickly and completely the new technology has taken hold. Under its influence, our industrial and business environment is changing rapidly. Combined with the economic upheaval through which we have been struggling in recent years, the implications for our human resources are far-reaching and critical.
More and more across the country, jobs are being defined using computer technology. Those of us not conversant with terms like Cobol, Pascal "C", Fortran, Bi Sync, Unix, and Ominel may react with the jitters when scanning today's roster of job qualifications.
Microelectronics will eliminate many unskilled and repetitive jobs, but it will create even more new and high-paying ones. In some cases, it will change the very concept of a skill. For example, with the transfer of a machinist's tasks to computer-controlled machines, the job of a machinist changes into one of monitoring the computer-controlled equipment. However, a machinist's job could be upgraded by combining his traditional mechanical skills with new computer skills. Much depends on how we choose to link existing skills with computer technology.
The high technology business is regarded as one of the healthiest and fastest growing. It is also widely recognized that Canada must encourage and support the growth of these industries to escape economic stagnation. So high technology is here to stay. As a woman, I recognize the usefulness of a microwave oven.
I feel we have to be optimistic about the changes occurring around us despite the growing pains and confusion that are part of this transition. At the same time, we have to be realistic enough to devise strategies that will overcome current problems and lay the foundation for the future labour market. An especially important strategy is to forge strong links between training and technology to overcome the skills gap and spur technological progress.
April 16, 1984

Good training programs that equip people to enter growth occupations temper their fears and anxieties about the effects of technology in the workplace. This makes training and retraining programs for new computer technology jobs both a social and economic necessity.
When all is said and done, skills are the building blocks of individual self-reliance and economic growth. They are the means of remolding our human resources to meet the new requirements. High levels of employment and productivity can be achieved if workers are equipped with the skills that will be in demand in the years to come. It is for this reason that the Government reorganized its training initiatives in 1982 and established the National Training Program.
The Government does intend to revamp the system where necessary and direct the bulk of federal funding to training high demand occupations. In the old days, some of our resources were clearly wasted on training for occupations which already had a surplus of skilled workers. We do not want that situation to recur. As a former president of a school board, I can remember this happening.
To prevent it, a number of initiatives have been set up under the National Training Act. These include the designation of occupations of national importance which are or will be in high demand and requires special training efforts to increase the supply of skilled workers. Sources of information in the federal and provincial governments and business and labour have been consulted to ensure that the list of occupations is on target. It will be reviewed and updated each year to reflect the changing labour market.
The need to channel workers into demand occupations is equal to the need to bring training facilities and equipment up to date. Undoubtedly, there is no point in designating occupations of national importance and embarking on a scheme to train people on sophisticated equipment which only a few facilities can afford. The Skilled Growth Fund is the obvious answer. The fund makes funding available to private and public non-profit organizations so that they can modernize facilities, buy equipment and develop courses to train Canadians in national occupations.

The need to set up a truly effective information system for the labour market is obvious to anyone who has ever had to determine manpower training priorities. Last year, the Government launched the Canadian Occupational Projections System for the purpose of undertaking the enormous and complex task of compiling and integrating data related to the labour market and obtainable from several sources in addition to the federal Government's own sources.
While this project is still in its early stages, it is already showing that it can be of great assistance in forecasting future manpower needs and identifying occupations where demand will be greater. Identifying and solving human resources problems will be vitally helpful in providing sound information
Supply
about the labour market. Seven workshops have been established throughout Canada to ensure the exchange of information necessary for such an effort. Representatives of the private sector and of the various levels of government will be meeting for a day or two in seven Canadian cities to identify regional and sectorial problems in order to obtain the most recent data on available human resources and to suggest how we should better orient our policies. In fact, one of these meetings will open tomorrow in Halifax.

The human resource workshops illustrate an important point. The Federal Government cannot do the job of developing Canada's labour force by itself. What is required is a combined operation involving all levels of government, business and labour. I am sure Hon. Members would agree that what we clearly need in this country is a continuing exchange of ideas and information, a partnership of dialogue in spirit. We also need to make a commitment to work together for economic growth as economic partners. We already have the instruments and agencies through which this can be done, but we must take advantage of every opportunity for meaningful contact.
Nowhere is the need for partnership as acute as in the sphere of human resource development. We all have a role to play in managing change, in rising to the challenge that change presents. The onus is on individual workers to train for new occupations. Unions must help their members to cope with the transition to new work environments. Employers must contribute to the training and development of their employees. Training institutions must ensure that adequate and relevant programs are available. All of us must work together to make it easier to adapt to change.
This Government has given top priority to involving business and labour as key players in resolving labour-market problems. We have not only worked with them in attempting to find the answers to problems, but we have been content to step aside while they jointly pool their expertise.
A prime example of this approach is the recently formed Canadian Labour Market Productivity Centre. The centre, although financed by the Government, will be a completely autonomous body, operated jointly by the Canadian Labour Congress and the Business Council on National Issues. It will be completely free from Government intervention to assess such issues as the impact of high technology on the labour market and of the need to increase industrial productivity.
This marks the first time in Canada's history that labour and management have had their every own mechanism for dealing together with matters of national economic importance. The centre's findings and recommendations will be eagerly awaited by Government. I take particular pride in the fact that I was a member of a government which was able to bring labour and management together in such a positive way. I should also add that I have been very impressed by the calibre of academics expressing interest in working for the centre or being kept informed of its findings.

Perhaps at this point I should mention the extent of our financial assistance for training. This fiscal year we will be spending more than a billion dollars to help Canadians upgrade their present skills or learn new ones. More than half the total training budget is directed toward the purchase of courses in both public and private learning institutions for individual Canadians. This will provide training opportunities for some 220,000 men and women, and nearly half of them will be young people.
Of course this billion dollar figure does not include the vast sums of money the federal Government channels into postsecondary education, much of which has a direct impact on preparing young Canadians for careers in such fields as computer programming. In addition, in recent years the federal Government has increased its grants to education councils so that more bright young Canadians can attain Ph.D.s in scientific and technical fields. To do so, the Government inspired itself with good reports like the one prepared under the chairmanship of the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. Allmand), the Dodge Report prepared in the Department of Manpower and immigration and the Wallace report on part-time and job-sharing. There was another good report prepared on educational leave.
This Government was very active in preparing for the jobs of tomorrow. We have also built training into our job creation and work-sharing programs. Two of our job-creation programs in particular, Career-Access and Job Corps, make it possible for young people to gain valuable on-the-job training. The work-sharing program has been modified to enable workers to take advantage of their day's off to undergo training. Once again we are taking the initiative in relating training to actual work situations.
I think in my remarks today I have shown how the Government is co-operating with the provinces, management and labour and develop training programs which will help individual Canadians adapt to rapid technological change. Many of the mechanisms we need, such as consultative processes, are already in place. Because of this, we are in a better position than ever before to modify our programs as required.
I was not impressed by the progress we have made in fostering provincial-federal co-operation in the training field. I was particularly pleased to respond positively to the suggestion that labour and education ministers meet before the fall to examine the recommendations of the National Advisory Panel on Skilled Development Leave, including the extent of illiteracy in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, some of the Opposition members may not be aware of recommendations concerning educational leave. Essentially, we are calling for a legislation which would give Canadians the right to accumulate educational leave credits with a view to acquire new skills while still earning a decent wage. I must stress that this kind of program exists in several
European countries. I suggest the same could be done here in Canada.
I believe we can no longer expect that people will acquire during the first 18 or 20 years of their life all the education they will need in their lifetime. Within an ever-changing labour market, studying is a continuing process which musts be extended to the whole life of workers. Government must find means and take steps to make such a process possible without affecting the individual's career.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would like to invite my hon. colleagues to avoid negative criticism of a program such as Summer Canada which will help thousands of young people. At a cost of $200 million, exactly 81,000 young Canadian students, through this program and through Youth Employment Centres, will have access to a summer job.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that the private sector has done its share last year by creating 330,000 jobs for youth. This was made possible by 1,600 young people who solicited these jobs, working within the Canada Employment Centres. I would like to remind the Hon. Member that this program enables young people not only to earn money to pursue their academic studies but also to gain experience which is a must. I deplore in these difficult times, especially hard for parents and young people, that Opposition members would reject any initiative taken by our youth. Young people may not be as experienced as their predecessors or their parents to establish a program and create jobs for themselves through the Summer Canada program; however, I can assure my colleague that 99 per cent of Summer Canada projects submitted are commendable initiatives and are quite remarkable efforts on the part of these young people. In my own riding, I can say that the work being done by these young people during the summer time enable them to pursue their academic studies and quite simply to gain a knowledge which they would not otherwise acquire through formal education.
I must remind my colleagues that I also call on the private sector to create jobs through the Summer Canada program. The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Hawkes:
That this House condemns the Government for its failure to work cooperatively with the provinces, business, labour, voluntary organizations and the educational community to provide adequate training and retraining opportunities that would enable Canadian workers to feel confident about their ability to deal with the challenges of rapid technological change.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of State for Youth (Mrs. Hervieux-Payette) has just spoken. I awaited with great anticipation some of her answers. I must say that I was very disappointed to hear more of what we have heard for the last 20 years.
Perhaps she did not even have the question.

That is right, perhaps she did not even have the question. When referring to technology she asked, "Where have Members of the House of Commons been?" We have already felt the impact on our side of the House. She has, we have, the whole country has, as have 1.5 million unemployed Canadians. We have all felt the impact. It is the impact of the neglect of the Government over the last 20 years. That is what
Supply
the impact is, that is what the neglect is, and that is the opinion of the public.
A good portion of those 1.5 million Canadian people are facing middle-age redundancy, and 500,000 young people do not even have an opportunity to face redundancy because they cannot find jobs in the workplace. However, they do face redundancy because their education has already proven to be inadequate and the possibility or probability for training or upgrading is closed to them. The Government has felt the impact, but why did it not do something about it? What did it do when it felt the impact?
Enrolment levels have increased of late. In other words, the youth of the country and those faced with redundancy are seeking ways through the educational system to obtain hopefully, retraining or a usefulness in the productive system. What does the federal Government do? It cuts back. The provinces will have less money for education because the Government brought in a Bill to reduce funding to educational institutions in Canada. Over the protests of the combined Opposition Parties, it forced the Bill through the House of Commons. There will not be more money to meet the training needs of these people next year, so that they will be equipped for the new technologies and new challenges. In fact there will be less. Of over $10 billion spent on unemployment last year, only 2.57 per cent went for training. I thought the Minister felt the impact. If so, how come only 2.57 per cent went for training?
One out of every five of those young people about which the Minister was speaking is today unemployed. They account for about 40 per cent of the total number of people unemployed in Canada. Of this 40 per cent, 73 per cent are at an educational level which does not exceed high school. We have read many reports about functional illiteracy. This Government two years ago, when facing this problem, showed great foresight and cut out all spending on training for basic literacy just to put these people back into the work force. We now have the impact.
I am disappointed, Mr. Speaker, in the Minister of State for Youth. She became defensive and described all the programs which Government had in place. But she did not listen to some of her own colleagues. We had a more honest and direct representation from the Hon. Member for Laurier (Mr. Berger). He indicated there had been a major drop during the last decade in the amount of moneys set aside for adult education and training. He saw this from the Government side of the House of Commons. He was a small voice back in the corner and the Government could not hear him. I hope that Hon. Member will hear our motion today, Mr. Speaker. I hope he will hear us address the basic problems, bringing forward some of the solutions which will, in fact, lead us into a better 1990 and beyond.
We should look at the solutions to this problems mentioned by the Minister. She announced that we were going to have a series of new meetings and workshops, city by city. That is commendable. She said we were going to have a new centre to study productivity. That is commendable. She said we were

going to have a national advisory panel on the subject. That is also commendable. She stood there and listed report upon report of things which could be accomplished, reports which are now sitting gathering dust on someone's shelf.
What the people of my riding want the Minister to know, and what the million and a half unemployed people in Canada want the Minister to know is that they cannot eat a report, Mr. Speaker. They cannot pay their mortgages with a conference. Students cannot pay their tuition fees with another meeting, with another conference or with another report. What we need, Mr. Speaker, is not more and more dollars spent on researching the problem. What we, in fact, need is action. We need action which is on the major economical ill which is facing the country.
I believe most of us have now identified that Canada's recovery is predicated on its capacity to increase its productivity. We must increase our productivity both in quantity and in quality on a per man, per hour basis. Once we increase that productivity, it is no good to store it in a granary somewhere, or in a warehouse somewhere, it has to be sold. It has to be sold on international markets.
Through that increase in productivity, through that trading and selling in international markets, jobs will be found, Mr. Speaker. But that is where jobs are also being lost. For every 1 per cent drop in international trade, we lose the equivalent of $6.5 billion, and that is not new trade which we cannot get, but trade which we used to have. Our share of world trade has dropped by 33 per cent, two and a half points. And that is where the jobs are lost and where the jobs must be found.
In our industrial, educational and job retraining strategies, we must recognize that that is where we must head. The orchestrated restriction to the flow of trade to Canada is threatening to wrap a tourniquet around Canada's lifeblood. The low level of research and development and the lack of retraining response to technological change has led to stagnation in our economy and to the high levels of unemployment which we all are experiencing and suffering.
The Minister is right, in that the post-industrial society has arrived and it is breaking all around us like a tidal wave. Canada has a nationwide need for retraining, innovation and research and development if we are to catch that wave towards prosperity. The challenge facing Canada is to apply new technology without massive job displacement and economic dislocation. Without the opportunity to meet and solve the challenges of that new technology, the work force will actively resist change. Therefore, we will have to work towards that change with new attitudes, new opportunities and new specific ideas.
The Hon. Member for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes), who has already spoken, did not just talk about reports. He has made his report and has suggested from his report specific lines of action. This comprehensive study on the problem of technological change for manpower and retraining is the first breath of fresh air this House of Commons has felt for a long time. It is that kind of breath of fresh air which is going to carry us forward into the next Government of Canada. If the
implementation of new technology means inevitably that some jobs will be lost, then those persons who are displaced must be adequately retrained so that they are full participants in the economic community.
Our Party has found that one of the main obstacles to solving the problem of technology lies in the vague wording of the Canada Labour Code, in particular, Sections 149 to 153. If you want an example, Mr. Speaker, of something which causes problems, which creates a tone of concern between labour and management, a lack of understanding, clarity and direction, it is the vague wording of the Canada Labour Code. The present Code does not satisfactorily address the problem of technological change today, much less the more comprehensive changes which will be required in the future. The present Code requires that the employer, who seeks to effect a technological change which affects the terms and conditions of security of employment of a significant number of employees, must give 90 days notice to the bargaining agent prior to the change.
I am not the first one, Mr. Speaker, on this side of the House to bring this problem to your attention. As I speak today, I want to recognize that this has been brought to your attention before by the Hon. Member for Perth (Mr. Jarvis), and I pay special tribute to him today for his distinguished parliamentary career. Hon. Members of the House will miss him. We wish him success. I hope that we will take the advice which he gave us as recently as a few months ago. He did address this problem but the Minister did not comment. Perhaps she should have talked specifically about what she can do now. She said she would listen to ideas from this side of the House but she did not listen to the Hon. Member for Perth. Perhaps she will listen today. We will try again.
This 90-day clause is of concern to us. The definition of technological change cannot possibly cover all types of changes in the way work is carried out as a result of new technology. However, the definition itself of technological change must be made more explicit. This section requires redress because the burden of proof lies on the employee to prove that the employer is introducing new technology and that it has an impact on his employment. The employee's task is virtually impossible if the employer does not provide the information on the change.
Phrases like "substantially and adversely affect" and "significant number of employees", are so vague that they do not allow the affected party to determine if notification is necessary. These phrases must be made explicit to avoid possible disputes that arise out of confusion because the definitions have not been clear. The opting out provisions of this section are unsatisfactory because they remove the compulsion to reopen bargaining. If an employer signs a collective agreement which gives notice of technological change prior to the conclusion of the last agreement, or has provisions which allow for the settlement of matters pertaining to technological change, or contains provisions to assist employees to adjust to the effects of changes, or if the agreement specifies that statutory provisions do not apply, then the employer does not have to
April 16, 1984

bargain with his employees. The problem is that both parties may not have had sufficient information on the impact of the change when the agreement was signed. Opting out also means that there is no mechanism for redress should a dispute arise.
As both I and the Hon. Member for Perth said, the 90 day notice period is simply too short to allow for negotiation of adequate adjustment policies or retraining agreements. Employers are not required to provide well detailed information of impending changes. A minor change like this sends out a signal to management and labour that we want to add clarity. From that we can add a tone of leadership which we can all co-ordinate to create this better environment we all know must be found in industrial relations.
Apart from the obvious negligence of the present Government in providing for adequate retraining programs, it is becoming increasingly apparent that our young people are not receiving the kinds of training they need in today's world. Canada suffers from a critical shortage of skilled workers in many sectors of the economy. Yet, in spite of those shortages, 1.5 million people are unemployed. Although international comparisons indicate that Canada has one of the world's best educated work forces, we are less well equipped educationally than some of our major competitors and the over-all trend is indeed discouraging.
For example, in our universities there are 200 vacancies in our management faculties, 200 in engineering, and 600 in computer science. We are graduating fewer Ph.D.s now in mathematics, engineering, agriculture and biological sciences than we did in 1974. Where is the direction, Mr. Speaker? Where is the leadership? In disciplines critical to our competitive future we are going backwards, not forwards.
The OECD estimates that between 25 per cent and 30 per cent of Canada's work force is functionally illiterate. The application of new technology will require higher levels of skill than our work force presently has. Clearly, with such a large functionally illiterate work place, the general knowledge will have to be increased before they can in fact develop the opportunities to participate in any new technological society to come.
We sit here and debate. We pile words upon words. It is like another report. I feel almost guilty doing it because I know that of the people in this House and those listening to us today there is not one person whose family is not touched by the impact of the technological society. There is not one person who does not know of someone who is unemployed, someone who has dropped out of school in grade 11, grade 12, is unemployed now and unemployed forever. He is cast from our society. I just wanted to end with the plight of that person listening today, Mr. Speaker. I urge the Government that now is the time for action, now is the time for programs. We are fed up with studies. We are ready to build a new country. I was going to detail the recommendations of the studies by the Hon. Member for Calgary West, but they are now public and available. We will send them wherever we have to. To him we offer congratulations, and we look forward to getting on with the job. There is new hope for that young person out there. It

I have listened with interest to the debate. Many of the things said by the Official Opposition and my colleagues in the NDP are things which I think most Canadians are anxiously awaiting to see from Government, whether it be federal or provincial. The Hon. Member who has just spoken and I both represent ridings in the Province of British Columbia. We all know that our forest industry is in some very serious trouble because of a declining timber base and world competition. The B.C. On The Journal he seemed to be indicating that they have all the problems solved and when they come to power there will be a great deal more confidence by Canadians in the country and in the world. Therefore jobs will automatically flow and there will be some incentives. Then we will have a big training program and everything will be solved.
I just could not believe that Canadian people are so ill informed that they would believe this. I do not think they will believe that the problems which are facing most of the industrial nations in the world will no longer face Canada because we will have a Government in which the world has the greatest confidence. I do not think people will believe that with some incentives and training everything will be fine, they will all have productive jobs and that this is the answer to the problem. I am not suggesting that some of these things are not needed. However, the utter simplicity of it baffled me. The people who were interviewing the Leader of the Opposition were having a great deal of difficulty believing what they were hearing as well.
I read 15 or 20 pages of the task force report on retraining. I think there is a good deal of merit in the report. I do not think it contains anything unusual or new. Its merit is in restating

some ideas which must be restated from time to time. I do not see anything basic in the report. I can accept the fact that all people on public assistance should have the opportunity for retraining. I can accept the idea that UIC funds should be devoted more and more to this and other purposes along this line. We on this side have been working on this for a number of years. I think there have been a lot of things done with the UIC dollar, including training.
The point of the matter is that the idea is not new. It is good to bring it up again and again to give it more emphasis, but I do not see that anything great is going to happen because of this report. It is not a new idea that we should be able to predict what kind of jobs are going to be available for people coming into the labour market and what kind of training is going to be required to equip people for these jobs. The Government itself set up a group called the Canadian Occupation Projections System, or COPS, with the idea of attempting to make these projections so that training programs can be organized correctly.
I have been wrestling with this problem for close to 30 years, both in this House and in the field of education before I came to this House. After 10 years of misinforming students I learned that this was not an easy question to deal with. We were always looking into the future and trying to get the best advice we could from our educational authorities, the provinces, and the federal Government, about the kinds of occupations that students could go into when they left school.
As soon as an operation becomes rather large, with many people employed in a specific area, such as when there was a great sudden demand for people in social work, there is a bulge in the system, and many are trained for this specific field but they find there are no jobs. This experience has led me, as a school administrator, to carefully consider the type of training to give students a chance to fit into the working community upon completion of that stage of their education. I came to the conclusion that it was a mistake to lead students or those returning to the educational system into a narrow occupational field, because very often the jobs in that particular field may not be available.
I have great concern that the emphasis in the last two years on high tech training to narrow, spin-off fields related to computer science could be carried to the extreme. However, I believe a general knowledge of computer science is important in order to be able to adapt when a particular computer field becomes crowded. When I see the number of students involved in the spin-off technologies of computer science, I question whether we are repeating what took place many years ago when far too many people were trained in the field of social welfare. While these people were eventually needed, they were employed elsewhere by the time the jobs were available. We should concern ourselves with general training rather than specifics. This report does make some suggestions in this respect, although I think many of us have already seen and acted on many of those suggestions.
Supply
We must also take into account the basic training that people need in order to fit into a world where they must be able to adapt or be retrained. We are told that some people may have to retrain three or four times in a lifetime. Thus, we should be concerned that people have the basic skills for this training and retraining. These discussions have not taken place in the House or among governments.
There have been some recommendations. First we must acknowledge that people must have a basic skill in such things as the English language and mathematics by the time they have completed Grade 11 or 12. In addition to these very important basic sills, one must include some general information about computer science, electronics and other components of the new world of high technology. I submit that people should not be trained at that point in their education to become specialists in a highly developed field, but be able to cope and understand the implications of the computer without necessarily becoming experts.
I fear that we may have already developed far too many specialists in certain branches of computer science. However, the era of high technology is something with which we must live. It is a new field that has added a dimension to our working world and many other aspects of our society. I believe we must have a good grasp of the fundamentals of this technology without being involved in specialization.
I am always concerned that people who are trained for a very highly developed field will have to start from the beginning if that field becomes obsolete or replaced. That should not be necessary. We should be able to train our students at a level which makes it relatively simple to move to a different field of which they have a basic knowledge.
There are many young people who, for various reasons, have not completed high school. There are good reasons why some people should not be taking secondary school at the time it is available to them. However, I find it is very common that these same people wish to complete their high school education later on when they feel they are ready to do so. We, as a Government, have attempted to encourage this.
The report discusses functional illiteracy. It is hard to believe that many people come under this category, as functional illiterates. Rather than condemn people for not completing high school when they had a chance, we should be ensuring the opportunity for them to return and complete the education that they missed. There are many reasons why people are wise to leave school at a particular point, and that is why I am disturbed that in the last two or three years governments at all levels have shown reluctance to deal with this particular kind of program.
While the report makes good suggestions with respect to functional illiterates, that term denotes one group of people, yet there are those who are relatively functional illiterates but do not fit into that category. They too must be trained to a point where they can move into more specific fields.
While much discussion has concerned training, it is only one solution, and perhaps may not even be a major solution for 1.5

Supply
million Canadians who do not fit into the labour force. While there is no question that the serious problem of training must be addressed, I had the impression, when listening to the Leader of the Opposition, that this was the answer; if there was confidence, incentives and training, everyone would be working and the problem would be solved. I do not see that happening. I envisage, and suggest, putting more money toward imaginative programs for training and retraining people. They should be prepared for the broad variety of experiences they will likely have in their lifetime.
I look back to the month of February. It was a typical kind of month in terms of jobs and employment. We had growth in jobs and in the number of people being employed. It was something in the order of 0.5 per cent, or, at the rate of 6 per cent a year. This is a very , very rapid rate of growth in jobs. If that could be sustained over a long period of time, we would be creating a large number of jobs. In round figures, it would be something like 60,000 jobs in that month. At the same time we had 0.5 per cent monthly or 6 per cent on an annual basis growth in jobs, we had a little over 7 per cent growth in the number of people in the labour force. Even with a 6 per cent growth in the rate of the creation of jobs we had an increase in the employment rate simply because more people were coming on the labour market than there were jobs being created. I suspect, and most people who think about this will say, that this will be continuous, particularly with the onset of more and more high technology. High technology will not create jobs. It will reduce the number of jobs available.
Nonsense.

One can expect over a period of time that growth in productivity will be attained by investment in high technology. But this will not satisfy the need for those people who want to work. I think we will find that high technology will replace many individuals. Therefore, some other alternative has to be considered.
I do not hear very much talk about things like renewing our forests and things of that kind which are tremendously important. Here we have a resource that exports in the range of $20 billion a year, more than agriculture, fisheries, and mining combined. We have not as a nation looked upon renewal of this resource, which is vital. In British Columbia if the resource is not renewed very shortly, we will not have an industry there. In Thunder Bay and throughout northwestern Ontario we have a situation which is very serious. In terms of the jobs that will have to be created to renew that force, these areas are labour intensive. It seems to me that is one of the areas at which we should be looking very seriously in terms of creating jobs.
I know the federal Government is in the process of putting together an agreement with the Province of Ontario and with the other provinces. I know the sums will be considerable, but even so, I do not think that will be great enough.
I know that my time is running out, but I would like to talk about the whole idea of work-sharing. I think the labour movement is pointing the way. We will have to start sharing work, perhaps by working shorter hours or taking early retirements. There may be many other ways in which work might be redistributed. I would like to discuss this at a later point.

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Hawkes:
That this House condemns the Government for its failure to work cooperatively with the provinces, business, labour, voluntary organizations and the educational community to provide adequate training and retraining opportunities that would enable Canadian workers to feel confident about their ability to deal with the challenges of rapid technological change.

Mr. Speaker, we are debating a motion today brought forward by the Official Opposition condemning the Government for its failure to establish adequate training programs in consultation with labour, programs which would fit Canadian workers to fill the jobs that will be created as a result of the introduction of new technology. We can support the motion, although to suggest that simply by a better system of training we will meet the problems of unemployment is oversimplifying the problem.
Let us look at the situation as it is today. At the present time there are 1.5 million Canadians unemployed, 40 per cent of whom are young people. There are probably another 200,000 or 300,000 unemployed who have not been counted because they are no longer looking for work; they have given up looking for work. Statistics Canada calls them the discouraged workers. The 1.5 million unemployed represents over 11 per cent of the labour force in Canada.
In 1969, a year after this Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) took office, only 4.4 per cent of the labour force was unemployed. According to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) this 1.5 million unemployed will continue to grow for the next number of years. In his Budget forecast, he predicted that unemployment would stay at the double-digit rate of 10 per cent or more for the next four or five years.
If one can believe what one reads, hears and sees, we are in the beginning of a second industrial revolution. The technological changes which have been brought about by the microchip and computer have begun to have marked effects on employment in this and every other industrialized country. The effects are just beginning. As the computer and microchip take over, there will be tremendous change. In the manufacturing industry, the robot, microchip and computer are taking over. Thousands of workers are being displaced, and not just the unskilled worker.
This raises the question of what even the best training system would do. Thousands of the most skilled workers we have known up to today are being thrown on the unemployment scrap heap. Machinists, tool and die makers, molders, are having their job done better, more efficiently and cheaper by the computer and microchip. I am sure there is not a Member of Parliament who has not seen what the new technology can do in their offices with the word processors, xerox machines and so on. Much more work can be turned out with the same number of employees, or even with fewer employees. In large insurance and trust company offices and in the offices
of all of the major industries and businesses which employ hundreds and thousands of people, it has been predicated by people who are knowledgeable and expert that hundreds of thousands of jobs will disappear. I have seen estimates which indicate that 40 per cent or more of these jobs filled almost exclusively by women will disappear in the next 10 or 15 years.
There has been an easy acceptance by many people in the Government and industry and, unfortunately in my view, by many academics that the era of high technology is coming and we cannot stop it. No one that I know of would want to stop it, but we are being told that it should be welcomed and that it will cause little if any dislocation. I am one of those who worry that the second industrial revolution which we seem to be entering will create as much havoc for the people of this country and every other industrialized country as created by the first industrial revolution. That revolution led to tremendous increases in productivity, but threw hundreds of thousands of people onto the scrap heap. In some cases, it took generations before these people were able to do productive work and live decent and comfortable lives.
If we are moving into a new industrial revolution, we must ask ourselves some very serious and fundamental questions. Let me pose three such questions about which we must think. First, how many new jobs will be created, and will as many new jobs be created in the new high technology industries as exist now in the traditional manufacturing industries? There is no indication that there will be as many workers employed in the new high technology industries as have been employed in the steel industries, the auto industry and the other industries in which so many of our people and the people of other countries have worked.
Second, we must ask ourselves where the new jobs will be located. It seems to me that if high technology industries do develop in Canada, it is likely they will be based in cities like Ottawa, where such a large proportion of the population is employed with the Government, and in cities like Toronto, Montreal and Vancouver. We must ask ourselves what will happen to the workers in the steel industry, for example. Will the steel industry in Canada suffer the same fate as the steel industries in the United States, France and Britain suffered? Even if productivity in that industry is higher than it was 10 years ago, employment has been reduced because of the use of new technology.
With the advent of new technology, what will happen to workers in Hamilton, Sault Ste. Marie and Sydney? What will happen to the farm machinery workers who live in Brantford? These are questions which must be addressed. If the old industries disappear, what will take their places in cities in which people have worked in the older mature industries for so many years?
Last, what wages or salaries will be paid to the people who will be working in the new high technology industries? Some studies have been done in the United States which indicate that in the new high technology industries the average wage is
April 16, 1984

$5,000 per year less than the average wage earned in the older manufacturing industries. That will have profound effects not only on the workers who will earn smaller wages but on all Canadians, because the purchasing power of the people who work in the new industries will be much less if we in Canada follow the same pattern as the United States.
The questions to which I referred are questions which must be addressed and understood, questions for which we must find answers. The Government has ignored these kinds of questions up until now and gives no indication that it will ever look at them seriously. From the Official Opposion, we get a motion which, if we can take it seriously, would seem to indicate that the only problem members of the Conservative Party see with the new technological takeover is that we have not trained people well enough. Of course we have not trained people well enough. Even if we had done so up until now, and even if we do so in the future, the fundamental problems which will be created by the introduction and wise use of new technologies will not be answered simply by providing training programs.
A famous American economist and Nobel prize winner, Wassily Leontief, when discussing the effects of new technology, said that he is afraid and predicts that the failure to redistribute the gains of automation and new technologies could condemn society to a paradoxical condition of rising productivity and rising destitution. There is no question that the new technology will permit and encourage a much greater level of productivity. However, hundreds of thousands of workers will be displaced and will have no jobs. As well, the people working in the new high technology areas will have to live with the lower wages paid. We in the New Democratic Party accept and support the motion which is before us today. Our training systems simply have not been good enough and are not good enough.
Let me take a moment to say that I was disturbed by the remarks of the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Atikokan (Mr. McRae). He spoke very briefly about illiteracy while ignoring the fact that if there is one area in which the federal Government has failed and ignored, it is the area of illiteracy. Looking at the training funds provided by the Department of Employment and Immigration over the last 10 or more years, one finds that less attention is paid and less money is allocated to training programs for basic skills education. The Hon. Member spoke about the millions of people who are functionally illiterate, but his Government, through its Department of Employment and Immigration, had ignored and thrown them on the scrap heap. The Government has refused to deal with this through training programs.
Let me make some very specific suggestions which we in the New Democratic Party believe need to be looked at in order to really face up to the problems of new technology.
We cannot deal with these questions without the fullest possible consultation among governments, federal and provincial, labour and management. We will not attain co-operation for any program if the people most directly affected have not
Supply
been consulted, such as the many young Canadians who do not have jobs or those who have had jobs and still have jobs but will be displaced by new technologies.
If we are serious about trying to deal with the new technologies, the first step which any government must take is toward real, meaningful and continuing discussions, consultations and planning on the part of labour, management, educational institutions and governments, federal and provincial.
What we have seen on the part of the Government has been ad hoc, hit and miss programs, in which the Government unilaterally, or sometimes in consultation with an industry group, brings in new programs such as ILAP. There are so many programs one could use every letter of the alphabet just to list them. That is one example of how the federal Government has completely failed.
The Government ought to look at making the Canada Pension Plan much more flexible. Workers, by increasing their contributions by a relatively small amount, should be able to opt for working part time at age 60 or 61. Perhaps they could work two or three days a week and receive the balance of their income, that is what they would obtain if they were working full time, from the pension plan. That could open up jobs for thousands of young Canadians who are now unable to find employment.
A similar idea would be to allow young parents of minor children to spend five years working part time but receiving full-time pay. It would be a good social policy. It would allow such parents to remain at home during the formative years of child rearing. At the same time it would provide additional employment for others in the workplace.
We need to look at what is happening in the economy at the present time. There has been a tremendous increase in the number of part-time workers. According to the statistics, in 1983 there were 400,000 fewer full-time jobs and an increase in part-time jobs of some 200,000. In the past 30 years, part-time employment has jumped from 4 per cent of the total work force to 16 per cent of all jobs in the economy. The new technologies will encourage and permit vast expansion in part-time work. With the shift to part-time work come the problems of the incomes of working people dropping. More and more part-time jobs are unorganzed, poorly-paid service jobs. People are being pushed out of the industrial sector of society by machines.
Both the Liberal Government and the Conservative Opposition stand on the same side of the fence. They put technology before people. If the companies benefit, those benefits should be shared by ordinary Canadians. That is the only acceptable policy. The policy of working with people and co-operating with business, labour and the provinces to develop programs which will put people first and machines second, will meet the needs of Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to pose a question to the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow). I find a lot of reason for pessimism in the presentation of the Hon. Member. He talked about worry, fear and somehow increasing the opportunity for employment without increasing the national well-being. He talked about work sharing and part-time work as if there were some magic pie in the sky banker who could finance it. He knows full well that if we do not increase our national productivity, we will not be competitive around the world. Canadians have lost 750,000 jobs in the last 10 years because our share of world trade in primary resource-based products has declined. The doomsayers have been around since the time of the industrial revolution, and I think we are hearing too much from them again.
There is hardly anyone in the country today who is not employed in a technologically-related job of one sort or another. It is not so much high technology or electronics that is of concern, it is the application of the technology to provide meaningful, long-term work for Canadians. Technology and its application are revolutionizing the world.
I am rather perplexed as to how the Hon. Member feels we should continue to enjoy the level of prosperity which he seems to take for granted when the country and the Government are near bankruptcy. How does he expect us to provide meaningful full-time jobs for Canadians unless we move into the technological era without fear or trepidation?

Mr. Speaker, I do not think the Hon. Member would find one sentence or paragraph in my remarks which would lead anyone to the conclusion that I oppose technological change or that I think we can somehow prevent it from taking place. We have to think about the results or the consequences of technological change. It is little comfort to steelworkers who have worked for 25 years, who have earned a good living and helped build the country, to be told that that industry can now produce as much or more steel with half the workforce of the past.
As I said, as we move into the technological revolution, we have to think of how the people who have been displaced will be able to work, produce, earn a living and live decent, comfortable lives. That is the point. Members of Parliament and everyone else must consider that problem. That is all I said. I did not suggest, nor would I ever suggest that we can or should stop this process. I have simply said that if it is to come about, it should be done with consideration for the people who will be adversely affected.

speechtext: Are there any more questions? On debate, the Hon. Member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Howie).

Mr. Speaker, whatever the specific detail of the present program structure, it is clear that the combination of government employment programs and the responses of the private and public sectors have not set in motion a sustained employment process in the have-not provinces of Canada.
The Atlantic provinces lead our nation in the human tragedy of more people seeking employment on a per capita basis than any other region of Canada. The hardship, frustration, disillusion created by lack of work and an inability to find employment are difficult to describe. However, possibly the most tragic dimension is the feeling of helplessness on the part of the head of the family who is unable to clothe, feed, house and educate his children properly. The impact on his children is a genuine cause for concern on the part of thinking Canadians everywhere.
The ugly tenacles of unemployment strike at single parent families, two parent families, widows, widowers, children, working mothers and working fathers. There are no exceptions to this human tragedy. There are a million and a half Canadians looking for work and another 300,000 who are not included in those statistics. Behind every such statistic is a human being worthy of the best efforts this Parliament can make in resolving this horrendous problem.
Recently in Saint John, New Brunswick, a new hotel opened offering 150 jobs. Two thousand people lined the streets of Saint John to apply for those jobs. In my constituency of York-Sunbury, because of educational, government, military and health institutions, we have a better employment rate than many parts of New Brunswick, if not all parts of that province. We also have 8,244 people collecting unemployment insurance benefits at the Fredericton office. These are active files on the roles today. The Youth Summer Employment Program which, like Career Access, is a good program, will employ 198 young people this summer. That figure will probably be increased by one-third because of the recent announcement by the Minister of State for Youth (Mrs. Hervieux-Payette).
Being an educational centre, my constituency has over 5,000 young people, many of whom will be looking for work in our community. I support every job-creation program which the federal Government announces to the very best of my ability, and I applaud every job which is created. However, I tell you frankly, Mr. Speaker, that with a slender private sector economy there are just not enough jobs to go around. Where hundreds of jobs are provided, thousands are needed.
We have to rejuvenate our country, offer hope instead of despair and rekindle the initiatives, energy and knowledge of our people. We must encourage the new technology to rebuild our competitive position, generate the resources to finance our economy and expand our international trade. We have the means to build a new Canada, a Canada of which we can all be proud, a Canada we can all feel part of, where we are happy and secure and in which we can have confidence for the future. There must be a massive commitment in co-operation with labour, management, and government at all levels, to the development of the most thoughtful and generous manpower retraining program which a civilized society has ever put together. More specifically, there are basic themes which form elements of that description. Development policies must contemplate a concentration on people and productivity as well as
April 16, 1984

on hardware and facilities. The key to the future is adaptation and innovation, product and process development and in techniques of management and marketing. We must promote a more effective role for smaller enterprises. We must recognize that the general level of skills in our population is inextricably linked to our rate of economic growth.
We have pursued the enhanced training of people in institutions but we have not always given appropriate attention to the need to relate certain kinds of training to the actual requirements of the work place. We need a very substantial emphasis on on-the-job training, not only in the conventional trades where this is already happening, but also in almost every other facet of enterprise. We must remember that training on the job uses industry as a carrier, and with the slender manufacturing base in the maritime provinces it does not address the need to the same extent as it does elsewhere in our country. This underlines the importance of institutional training and training in small businesses in the maritime provinces, and underlines also the tragedy of the fact that now that Bill C-12 is passed, each of the maritime provinces receives less money for educational training than it would have received if Bill C-12 had not been passed.
An altered view of the role of educational institutions to increase their relevance to community and economic development requirements is important. For example, an increase in emphasis on continuing adult education, and a design of business administration programs which have a greater small business orientation, are possible directions. Here I would like to commend the Hon. Member for Laurier (Mr. Berger) on his observations on the major drop during the last decade in money set aside for adult education and training.
A major theme which is essential is the need to adapt to changing conditions. We need new programs to encourage innovation in business such as a better transfer of information between the patent and licensing office in the business community in order to promote new technology. We need grants to industry and trade associations to promote and cost-share the running of management training seminars. Among other things, these seminars would familiarize business men and women with existing government programs. We need incentives to increase the supply of risk capital in underdeveloped areas. We need an expanded and altered mandate for research and further incentives to encourage process redesign and innovation. We need a stronger marketing orientation in the program structure specifically aimed at more effective penetration of local, regional, national and international markets. We need an improvement of incentive programs, enriching location grants for target industries and allowing tax holidays for companies locating in underdeveloped regions. We need an altered view of competition and of the role of the smaller enterprises.
Small production units are characteristic of the maritime provinces, and good export performance, effective research and development are often absent and require economies of scale. We need to achieve such economies but without, at the same time, destroying the distinctive positive qualities of smaller
