enterprises, effective employment generation, adaptability and responsiveness. We have to supplement our heavy emphasis on natural resources, at least in part, by an emphasis on people's skills and productivity.
Although we have perceived the need to move beyond the traditional industries, we have not always moved into better production in marketing techniques, more sophisticated higher quality versions of existing products, new products related to our existing basic skills or material expertise in marketing channels. We gain little when our agricultural products are shipping outside New Brunswick to be purchased back later as canned vegetables, meats or jellies, with good jobs going to other areas. We gain little when our forest products are shipped abroad to be purchased later as furniture and building materials. Deck hardware, navigational aids and fishing gear are purchased but not always manufactured in New Brunswick. More of these products should be manufactured in that province and more jobs should be created for the people of New Brunswick.
Building on our competitive advantages of resources, location and market access, we have done a great deal. The Japanese, however, have taught us that we can be successful without an abundance of material resources when people and organizations work together, particularly in the information economy. In order for people to receive the benefit of new technologies and advancement, it is essential that policies be developed in advance to enable the new technology to improve and expand the economy in order that more jobs can be created to offset the current trend of seeing jobs lost through mechanization.
Although federal initiatives, like the Skills Growth Fund program, provide an opportunity to offer advanced technological training, the difficulty remains that in a province like New Brunswick, and other small provinces, it is difficult to avoid coping with a continually changing list of nationally designated occupations, to the extent that we often have very little lead time between when occupations are newly designated and when training in those occupations must be delivered.
The relationship between technological change, employment maintenance and human resource planning is highly complex. In the case of New Brunswick, this complexity is further heightened by the lack of information which enables us to define with reasonable accuracy the economic sectors and activities in which technological applications should be actively encouraged, and to forecast the accompanying human resource needs. Clearly, the province's small population and economic base dictates that resources should be focused wherever our natural advantages would give our industries an optimal chance for success, and this focus should extend far beyond the technological field per se.
Against this background, the fundamental need for New Brunswick, the maritime provinces and Newfoundland, at this point is for quality information upon which we can base our training or retraining responses to technological change, and the financial resources to program effectively those responses.

April 16, 1984
Supply
On another aspect of this problem, there are two buzz words in Japan today that no self respecting small city mayor dares ignore: technopolis and teletopia. The words sound grand and futuristic but the idea behind them is simple. Japan's government wants to take high technology rapidly to the underdeveloped corners of the country and is designating a string of outlying model cities as a way of getting it there. Some will essentially be high tech industrial parks and research centres. Others will be fitted with advanced communication systems linking businesses, homes and government offices.
The technologies envisioned for the revamped communities are generally no more advanced than those found in North America today, and despite the space age titles, designated communities are not expected to become pioneering examples of urban design. What is expected is that promotion of high technology in communities off the beaten path will encourage Japan's unified entry into a new era of advanced industry and communications. Industries are to include electronics, biotechnology, software development and robotics. These will also include interactive video systems, high speed computer communications, expanded use of fibre optic cable and teleconferencing.
Communities like those in New Brunswick and the other Maritime Provinces will be allowed to offer special tax breaks and low interest loans to high tech companies locating in their industrial parks. The first group is scheduled for completion in 1987 when upgrading roads and airports, new housing and facilities for research staff and a core of high tech industries are to be in place. This is indeed good planning, and we should take a page out of the Japanese book, and take it now. It requires a conscious decision of government to bring it about and that decision should be taken now.
Finally, I feel we should significantly expand wage subsidy programs such as the career access program. We should institute a program of refundable employer tax credits. We also have to provide training and retraining in high technology skills in order to avail ourselves of the jobs that do exist. We have to work with universities, industry and labour, to ensure that Canadians are not victimized by technological change. We have to act long before the changes take place.
We have to greatly improve information exchanges through which people become aware of job opportunities. Too many young people graduate from training programs and cannot find work, not because their skills are not in demand, but because they cannot make contact with the employer who needs them. We have to remedy this defect. We have to institute programs specifically designed to address the chronic unemployment which tragically plagues certain regions of Canada like the Maritimes.
In the Province of Newfoundland 37 per cent of young people, that is 37 per cent of persons between 15 and 24, who were seeking work are without jobs. In New Brunswick and Nova Scotia the figure is 27 per cent, and in Prince Edward Island, 26 per cent. Wage subsidies and refundable employment tax credits are good incentives but may not always be of
maximum benefit in these regions because of the slender industrial economy. Therefore, in these areas we should also institute programs of community based entrepreneurial development. We have to assist individuals and groups wishing to start new enterprises to raise capital, cut through red tape, indentify markets, train workers and establish constructive working relationships with local workers, educators and financial institutions. We have to offer what has been denied over half a million young unemployed Canadians and a million adults-a future.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this discussion, I feel that I am fulfilling my first and foremost duty as a parliamentarian.
Can there be a more serious problem or a greater tragedy than that of a man or a woman who cannot earn a decent living or make a contribution to his or her family and to society? On the other hand, is there a more difficult problem to solve than that of reducing the current unemployment levels?
I have been listening since this morning to all those who have taken part in this debate and I have a feeling that we are all convinced of the seriousness of the situation and worried by the lack of any genuine solution to the problem. I am giving all the Members, wherever they may be sitting in this House, the benefit of the doubt, and I know they realize that, faced with such a serious problem which has reached proportions that can only be termed as tragic, what is most important is to call on the goodwill of everyone in this House and every group in our society, including the employers, the unions, the voluntary organizations, as well as the provincial, federal and municipal governments. People tend too easily to apportion our collective responsibility where unemployment is concerned. This is probably the basic reason why ideological, partisan and jurisdictional walls prevent us from doing anything and this is a failure we must all admit in the face of the increasing number of unemployed. I would like to invite my colleagues in this House, where we often have more work than we can handle, to make a collective effort to co-operate and face this increasingly serious problem of unemployment.
Mr. Speaker, one thing I do appreciate today is to be among my friends and former co-members of the task force on job opportunities for the eighties. I know the sponsor of today's motion, my colleague and friend, the Hon. Member for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes). I am sure his intentions are good, but I would have liked him to be less radical in the wording of his motion. If the Hon. Member for Calgary West had simply said that the Government should do more to co-operate with voluntary organizations, business, labour and the educational community to provide adequate training and retraining opportunities that would enable Canadian workers to have confidence in their ability to deal with the challenges of fast technological changes, if these simple words had been used to
April 16, 1984

ask for the co-operation of both sides of the House, I would have been happy to support the motion. However, I still agree with the thrust of the motion, which calls for this co-operation which I mentioned earlier, this co-operation which is the only way to bring about the decrease in unemployment that we all want.
Of course, this debate provides us with a golden opportunity, Mr. Speaker, as we are given a chance to refer to the amount of $ 1.2 billion that the Canadian Government is allocating this year to the important area of occupational training under its new National Training Program.
Naturally, nothing is perfect, especially when technological changes are causing an upheaval in the industrial sector. It is precisely for the purpose of discussing possible improvements to this program and other initiatives developed in co-operation with the Provinces that the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Roberts) has announced right here in this House that he intends to have further discussions with his provincial counterparts in June or July of this year.
On the other hand, Mr. Speaker, this very interesting debate also concerns, rather strangely in my opinion, what the Official Opposition considered last week as an occupational training program, which they did not however call official and whose costs they certainly did not reveal. According to the Members opposite, this program would bring about a phenomenal increase in the number of jobs for reasons which remain totally unexplained except in the sense that it calls for a change of Government.
Yet, Mr. Speaker, I think that, on both sides of the House we all know that a change of Government does not constitute a solution in the eyes of the public. The polls show that, no matter which party is in power, the current serious unemployment problems would still exist. These problems exist because of the international juncture, the conditions prevailing in the United States, and the situations locally and regionally.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to appeal to my friends opposite, some of whose comments I have found very offensive. When my friends opposite ask for the elimination of some job-creation programs such as Canada Works or summer programs, I am ready to give them the benefit of the doubt. However I would like them to understand that in remote areas such as ours, particularly in these difficult times, the only solution is job-creation programs providing temporary work. Of course, they are not permanent jobs, but they give needy families the support and assistance which would otherwise be denied to them.
My friends opposite are inclined to plan their programs and their action for large cities. Big cities certainly play an essential role in the future of a country such as ours. However, I would like to remind all members of this House that in dynamic areas such as the one I have the honour to represent
Supply
and in several others if not throughout the country, we usually find the vitality, the inventiveness, the spontaneity, the devotion and the labour necessary to keep and preserve a country as great as ours.
I make this appeal, Mr. Speaker, because I know that not only the members opposite but also some government members often take this attitude which I find disturbing when they feel that the answer to a problem is solely to be found in urban centres. I do not deny their importance and value but I think that they can only provide a partial answer.
When we find Canadians at work throughout the land, from coast to coast, our country will then be thriving, having recovered its strength and vigour. I am sure that it will recover in the years to come for in spite of our present problems. I have confidence in our future.
Mr. Speaker, in this program that is put forward by our friends in the Official Opposition, a program which they had the opportunity to discuss and refine over a weekend, I find that there are, on the one hand, some aspects which are already in force and on the other hand, some other aspects which seem unfeasible to me. For example, Mr. Speaker, the Progressive Conservative Party has suggested that we provide for the creation of education savings plans, contributions to which would be tax-deductible as is the case for Registered Home Ownership Savings Plans. This kind of proposal obviously benefits higher income earners. In fact, the National Training Program already entitles people in training to direct financial aid equal to tuition fees. In my view, this is a completely different and more satisfactory method than the one recommended by Official Opposition members.
Let me give another example, Mr. Speaker. The Progressive Conservative Party has recommended the federal Government give loan guarantees to people in need in order to enable them to benefit from training and other educational programs. Yet, lowest income earners are not even required to pay registration fees for these institutional training programs. They receive an allowance equal to tuition fees.
Mr. Speaker, the Progressive Conservative Party has also recommended that fiscal incentives be given to employers to compensate for the cost of training and retraining of their employees. Yet, the Industrial Training Program already provides for direct reimbursement to employers of most of their training costs as well as half the trainee's salary. Training costs are already tax-deductible at the present time. I could list a dozen other examples of this kind, which would confirm that some of the proposed solutions are already in place.
Will all due respect for my friends opposite other proposals seem unfeasible in my view.
I have noticed, with considerable pleasure, that several of the solutions listed in the Conservative program originated from the task force in which we had participated and which I have referred to. I know that the hon. member for Calgary

April 16, 1984
Supply
West was a member of that task force, together with others, such as the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) who made his comments a while ago. His contribution was very much appreciated, and so was the contribution of the hon. member for Brampton-Georgetown (Mr. McDermid) who also did an excellent job. Partisanship has its place on certain occasions of course, however I feel that in this instance we have put forward very interesting solutions which have resulted in 186 resolutions now partially implemented. And when the hon. member for Winnipeg North asked a while ago just how many resolutions had been implemented, I felt that was a very relevant question I should direct to the Minister of Employment and Immigration.
Getting back to other suggestions from the Opposition, already implemented in the training programs, Mr. Speaker, there was the idea of using the Unemployment Insurance Fund. That is now a reality, for $259 million from the Unemployment Insurance Fund will be used this year for training purposes. And that, not to mention the federal contribution to a Quebec pilot assistance project for young welfare recipients under the Begin-Marois agreement. Recently I had the opportunity to comment on this and emphasize the fact that we are contributing $58 million over a two-year period to cover at least 50 per cent of the costs involved in the Quebec program which aims at helping young welfare recipients who are able to work.
In the Opposition scheme many references are made to the tax cuts and special incentives for the purchase of equipment and improvement of training courses. This suggestion is already being implemented, Mr. Speaker, thanks to a properly operating formula. I am referring to the Skills Growth Fund through which we will pay directly for this year alone, $86 million to teaching and training institutions to up-date their equipment and training facilities and overcome the serious skill shortages resulting from technical and technological changes.
In that respect, Mr. Speaker, I would like to quote from a special article on robotics by Mr. Lucien Piche published in the April issue of the Commerce magazine, which I have just received and had a quick look at. The author talks about the "handouts contributed to the CEGEPs by the federal government", and goes on to say, and I quote: "since the Canada-Quebec agreement on adult occupational training was concluded in 1982-83, the CEGEPs have been literally showered with grants. The Skills Growth Fund established by the federal Manpower Department in February 1983 has already agreed to some Quebec projects for a total of $36 millions." In the few seconds left to me, Mr. Speaker, I would simply point out that the Jonqui&re CEGEP had submitted a projet. As you know, those projects must also be approved by the Quebec government. However, due to the latter's inaction and obstruction, the Jonquiere CEGEP lost $2 millions because the Quebec government refused to give the go-ahead already given by Ottawa.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I hope that all Hon. Members will put partisanship aside and will turn with confidence to the
future, all working together to reduce, if not elimininate this tragic problem of unemployment all across Canada.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Are there questions or remarks?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with great interest to what my colleague had to say about the Skill Growth Fund.
On the basis of the motion now before us, I would like first to ask him a question about his region. About the Jonqui&re CEGEP, can he tell us in fact, in what field did the CEGEP in the riding which he has represented in this House for several years now, want to specialize? And is it not one of the programs launched by the federal Government through the Ministry of Employment and Immigration to encourage people to further their schooling in that high technology field and to make sure that educational institutions offer students courses preparing them for the labour market where new technologies are in demand?
I know that for some time now there is in his riding a new pulp and paper mill, which belongs to a company from the Eastern Townships; high technology has surely some importance in the project. The Papier Cascade company bought a plant in his region and he talks to us about the CEGEP. Can he tell us in fact if, contrary to what the opposition says, the federal Government, through the Skills Growth Fund in the case of the Jonquiere CEGEP, would have not agreed, had an agreement with the Quebec Government been secured, to a request for a job creation program in high technology because in his riding as well, they are trying to overcome unemployment and to improve their economic situation?

Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank the Parliamentary Secretary for his excellent question, and commend him for his work as Parliamentary Secretary.
I would like to suggest that I am quite pleased indeed that he touched on the matter of Papier Cascade taking over a plant in our area. The Lemaire brothers, as they are called, are Quebec leaders, people with entrepreneurship, and I am very happy with this takeover. The Canadian Government contributed $1,250,000, and I think this bodes well for the future.
In answer to the Hon. Member, I must state that what the Jonquiere CEGEP proposed was a training capacity increase in the area of computer assisted design and manufacture.
That proposal had been developed over many months. It enhanced the Jonquiere CEGEP, which is playing a major role in that area on the regional level.
This was an opportunity for people in Jonquiere, especially the CEGEP people, with the help and assistance of local firms, which brings us back to the motion now before us-local people as I said, whether Alcan or Price, to show they were interested in working very closely with the CEGEP to put in place those facilities so that our young, may get involved and work in keeping with technological change.
April 16, 1984

Therefore, this was an excellent opportunity for local heads of institutions of higher learning, and also young people to show that it is not only in larger cities that major projects can be launched. And the Government perhaps did more, by recognizing the needs of our regions and ensuring that in communities such as ours, people do not feel left behind. The Development Fund Progam would have made the implementation of this project possible.
Unfortunately, Quebec said no! It is our hope they will change their minds, because we are going to put forward another proposal. We will not let matters stand. We are going to try again, and it is our hope that Quebec will bear reason, at least for once.

subtopic: IMMIGRATION-REPLACEMENT OF COURT REPORTERS WITH RECORDING DEVICES IN IMMIGRATION OFFICES. (B) QUALITY OF TRANSCRIPTS PRODUCED FROM TAPE RECORDINGS
IMMIGRATION-REPLACEMENT OF COURT REPORTERS WITH RECORDING DEVICES IN IMMIGRATION OFFICES. (B) QUALITY OF TRANSCRIPTS PRODUCED FROM TAPE RECORDINGS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on January 30 I asked a very straightforward question of the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Roberts) regarding changes in staff and staff policy in immigration offices. What is proposed is that some very skilled court reporters who work in refugee and immigration hearings be replaced by transcribing machines from which the court records would subsequently be typed by typists at a considerably lower rate of pay.
There are two problems with this policy of the Government. One is that women will lose more skilled jobs at a higher rate of pay, and be replaced by machines and other employees at a lower rate of pay. The other is the quality of the work itself. Peoples' lives depend upon accurate records for immigration and refugee status hearings. The quality of product which comes by the use of machines without having a person there to check on the material has been found wanting. We know from other places, that the records are not adequate and have caused problems.
The Minister said he would look into the matter. The union is pursuing it. There has been a grievance on the question. The grievance has now gone through two stages and has been turned down. It seems the department is going ahead to replace these skilled women with machines and other employees at a lower rate of pay. We have not managed to stop that.
Adjournment Debate
I would like to point out, Mr. Speaker, that throughout all of this the department concerned has a policy on technological change. It has a personnel policy which would direct it in quite a different way. Let me quote from that policy:
The Canada Employment and Immigration Commission/Department recognizes that technological change, and technological improvements generally, offer great scope and the ideal opportunity for the organization to not only improve the quality of the services and programs it offers to the Canadian public, but also to extend the capabilities and opportunities available to its staff and, to the fullest extent possible, improve the quality of the Commission/Department's work environment for the benefit of all employees.
Yet, here we see some employees who will be clearly disadvantaged by these changes which are in process, and certainly the quality of the service will go down. Let me continue quoting from the policy:
In order to ensure that the maximum benefits to be derived from the application of technological change are earned and shared by all staff, the Commission/Department is fully committed to ensuring that the introduction of such changes in its work locations are both approached and accomplished in a manner which will minimize any possible adverse impact for employees whose work environment is to be affected.
Then it says there will be full consultation with representatives of the employees at all organization levels.
Further, the policy goes on to specify a number of principles which must be respected. It states that full and ongoing consultation to ensure the negative impact of the introduction of technological change on long-term employment is kept to an absolute minimum. Employees affected by the introduction of new technologies will be provided with an opportunity to acquire the necessary knowledge and skills to enable them to take advantage of new jobs emerging from technological change. But here we have people being deskilled; not being trained to do more difficult and higher paid jobs, but being deskilled. That is the opposite to what the department talks about when it has its fine principles on paper.
Further, this same department has an affirmative action program. Here we have a lovely affirmation action program, but it is on paper. It talks in very fine language: "It is our intention through this program to eliminate employment barriers faced particularly by women and other groups." It talks about the need for a stronger commitment on the need of federal employees to eliminate discrimination or discriminatory employment practices and develop a work force that is representative of the work force of the public it serves. Yet while it talks about all this, it is going in precisely the opposite direction, deskilling jobs, seeing that women have fewer job opportunities than in the past.
One job opportunity that has become open at the same department is for immigration counsellors. The first job description for this would have screened out these very women who are losing their jobs through technological change. Fortunately the employment and immigration union of the Public Service Alliance of Canada fought this procedure and a new definition for the job search has been set up. These women will now have a chance to apply for these jobs. That is a very

April 16, 1984
Adjournment Debate
small victory indeed. The very fact that this had to be fought so that women would have an opportunity to apply for these better jobs shows the mentality of the Department.
Finally, other people will suffer as well as the employees. The records that come out of these tribunal hearings are enormously important. Refugee and immigrant status will depend on what is written down at these hearings. This is supposed to be a service to the public. It is absolutely vital. Where machines are being used in other places there are notations of "inaudible", "sic", misspellings and all kinds of problems that lawyers for the people concerned have noted with the record. I urge very strongly that this matter be reconsidered, that the deskilling end and that quality service be provided by the Department for the people so vitally concerned.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jean-Guy Dubois (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
subtopic: IMMIGRATION-REPLACEMENT OF COURT REPORTERS WITH RECORDING DEVICES IN IMMIGRATION OFFICES. (B) QUALITY OF TRANSCRIPTS PRODUCED FROM TAPE RECORDINGS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to elaborate on the answer given by the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Roberts) to the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald) on January 30, 1984.
There are 19 court reporters in Toronto and 15 in Mississauga, all of them classified ST-COR-1. Under the Commission's global strategy to reduce by March 31, 1987 the backlog of enquiries and applications for refugee status, the Ontario region plans to install electronic recording equipment in all courtrooms and to hire typists to transcribe the recordings which now exceed present capacity. The executive director for the Ontario region met with union representatives on December 6, 1983, in order to get their views on technological change. Later, on December 16, he confirmed the following in writing to Mr. William Fisher, Regional Manager of the Employment and Immigration Union, and I quote:
As far as implementation of electronic recording in the immigration group is concerned, and in accordance with clause 9 of the ST collective agreement dealing with technological change, I am pleased to confirm the commitment I gave your Union at our meeting. Management put in use electronic recording equipment to process enquiries and assess applications for refugee status in order to reduce serious backlogs in the Ontario region and particularly in the immigration districts of Toronto and Mississauga. Additional resources have been allocated for the present fiscal year and other resources have been requested for 1984-85 and 1985-86 in order to help with recruiting clerk-typists and take care of the backlog before March 31, 1986. Court reporters working presently with the Department will still record enquiries using either head phones, a transcription machine or shorthand and will then type required texts. Classification level for court reporters will not change. They will keep their status of employees hired for indefinite period and will still get the pay rate applicable to court reporters in the ST category.
Grievances were filed following that decision and they are being dealt with according to established rules. Besides, a study is being made of means to give present reporters the benefit of some opportunities for promotion. In the meantime, it is believed that the union had ample opportunity to make its
opinion known on that matter and that the requirements of the ST's collective agreement regarding technological change were complied with. Those consultations were also held according to instructions pertaining to technological change in EIC and the policy relating to personnel. The training aspect has also been considered, because management has promised to make sure employees will be taught how to use more sophisticated typing and reproduction equipment when it becomes available.
In conclusion, as concerns the quality level of the work done with this equipment, the Quebec Region has been using it for several years now and no loss of transcription quality has been detected. So I hope this fully answers the Hon. Member's question.

subtopic: CANADA POST CORPORATION-REQUEST FOR CANCELLATION OF CONSUMERS DISTRIBUTING PROJECT. (B) REQUEST THAT PROJECT RESULTS BE RELEASED PUBLICLY
CANADA POST CORPORATION-REQUEST FOR CANCELLATION OF CONSUMERS DISTRIBUTING PROJECT. (B) REQUEST THAT PROJECT RESULTS BE RELEASED PUBLICLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I directed a question to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) today in the absence of the Minister responsible for Canada Post. My question regarded the expansion of Canada Post service as it relates to Consumers Distributing, a direct invasion into the private sector. This invasion has been opposed by government Members as well as by members of the Conservative Party.
I would like to read into the record tonight some of the concerns of interested parties. We have received correspondence from Home Hardware in Souris, Manitoba. That letter reads:
Why should I, as an independent retailer, subsidize through my tax dollars a large company like Consumers (Distributing)?
The Canadian Retail Hardware Association which has member stores right across Canada points out the following in a letter of March 1, 1984:
The members of this association-over 2,000 hardware and home centre stores across Canada-will be significantly and adversely affected by this move. On their behalf, we register extreme displeasure and plead for an immediate review of the policy which has allowed such an "arrangement" to develop. Our concern is centered in three distinct areas:
1.	The entry of Canada Post into this area does not serve any demonstrated need of the Canadian public. There is then, no reasonable rationale for a Crown corporation to enter this area of free enterprise.
2.	The existence of Canada Post offices in virtually every community of Canada would immediately give one player in the competition game-Consumers Distributing Limited-access to all of these markets. The other players in the game in each of those markets is required to make significant community investment. The competitive balance will be upset. Legitimate retail businesses will suffer.
It is not the purpose of Government, Mr. Speaker, to be interfering in the private sector in the first place. I shall continue reading from the letter:
3.	Canada Post has monopoly power to provide normal postal service in Canada. The monopoly implies an obligation on Canada Post to provide the best postal service of which it is capable. It is clear that Canada Post needs to concentrate on improving its level of service in postal handling and delivery. This is the challenge which should preoccupy postal authorities.
April 16, 1984

I could not agree more.
A letter to the President of Canada Post from the Pembroke City Council was reported in the Pembroke Observer of March 20,1984, and reads as follows:
A meeting of the Pembroke and area Chamber of Commerce representing the interest of over 250 member businesses, was convened on March 9, 1984, to discuss concerns with regard to the pilot project recently undertaken by Canada Post and Consumers Distributing.
During the meeting it was decided that: whereas Canada Post was established and capitalized by the taxpayers of Canada,
Whereas! the traditional mandate of Canada Post is to operate an adequate mail delivery service,
Whereas we believe the aforementioned pilot project is not in keeping with this mandate and is in fact an unwarranted intrusion into the private sector,
Whereas we strongly believe this arrangement will result in a reduction in the quality of the postal service,
Therefore we must vehemently oppose this type of arrangement and request that it be discontinued immediately.
I believe that it should be discontinued immediately, Mr. Speaker.
In the March 20, 1984 edition of the Pembroke Observer the following letter to the President of Canada Post from MPP Sean Conway appeared:
I wish to express my strongest disapproval of the arrangement which Canada Post has struck with Consumers Distributing to participate in their mail order business. I do not think it proper for a Crown corporation to involve itself with a private company actively competing with local businesses. If Consumers Distributing wishes to establish in the Pembroke area, we would be pleased to welcome them as a free standing enterprise. If however, Consumers Distributing is to enter our market area as a subsidiary of Canada Post, then such an arrangement is unfair and unacceptable. Tax paying local businesses should not be forced into competition with a joint venture which they are, in fact, subsidizing.
Also the following was reported on CHRO News in Ottawa on March 20:
Today, when the agenda of the Chamber of Commerce meeting in Pembroke turned to Canada Post's experiment with Consumers Distributing one could feel a definite charge run through the rooms. These people, many of them small business operators, are angry. They feel that having Consumers Distributing in the post office is the same as government subsidized competition. The Chamber received five more letters today from business people and consumers opposed to the experiment and correspondence was produced from one of the Quebec communities involved in the Canada Post experiment. The Chamber's President stated "We've just received a letter from Noranda and I'm glad to say that it's not only ourselves in Smiths Falls in Ontario that are objecting but also the test areas in Quebec. They have circulated a petition in their area and we're hoping to do the same."
Some of the correspondence I have received as official spokesman of the Opposition of Canada Post has come from cities such as Pembroke and Smiths Falls, from Home Hardware, the Canadian Retail Hardware Association and the Canadian Federation of Independent Business. Other individuals have written from across Canada. Mr. Speaker, I am sure you are also receiving mail in opposition to this intrusion into the private sector.
A letter to the Canadian Retail Hardware Association from the Chairman of the Board of Canada Post indicated:
The advent of new technologies will compel the corporation to alter its services in the future. If the corporation is to become self-sufficient, it is necessary that we do more than solely deliver "traditional" forms of mail.
Adjournment Debate
They will be stopping the private sector from becoming self-sufficient. I suggest that the Government should force Canada Post to drop this proposal.

speakeroldname: Mr. Normand Lapointe (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Labour):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
subtopic: CANADA POST CORPORATION-REQUEST FOR CANCELLATION OF CONSUMERS DISTRIBUTING PROJECT. (B) REQUEST THAT PROJECT RESULTS BE RELEASED PUBLICLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to clarify the matter raised by the Hon. Member and to disprove certain erroneous ideas about the services that have been tested by the Canada Post Corporation in co-operation with Consumers Distributing.
First, Mr. Speaker, let me state once again the three main objectives which the Parliament of Canada has set for the Canada Post Corporation. Here they are: the Corporation must enhance the postal services, bring labour relations into line, and attain financial self-sufficiency.
As you can see, Mr. Speaker, the legislation that established the Canada Post Corporation provides that it must become financially independent. Besides, what matters is that in several areas, emphasis is being laid on the need to keep up with the times and supply products and services best suited to the requirements of the Canadian people.
Canada Post Corporation is responsible for the operation of a postal service involving the collection, transmission and distribution of messages, courriers, monies and commodities without accountability. It is expected, of course, to adjust to the changing needs of the Canadian users.
The tentative services which were set up in co-operation with Consumers Distributing and its clients is only the harbinger of what will be common practice in the 21th century. That company realized that postal services have always been a good publicity medium and have always managed to dispatch direct postal orders, money orders or parcels efficiently. By developing new processes, the Corporation has been able to offer new services specifically designed to Consumers Distributing and generate new revenues.
Canada Post Corporation is not doing at all what the hon. member is suggesting. It did not move into the retail business. It does not buy, own, stock or sell commodities and it does not offer any warranty or install material. In other words, it does not do the retailer's job. It dispatches written material, monies and parcels and carries out activities which have always been the responsibility of the post office for the last two centuries.
If we are to consider Canada Post as a retailer-

INCOME TAX ACT-TAKING OF TAXPAYERS' STATEMENTS UNDER OATH-MINISTER'S POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on March 22, I asked the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Bussieres)

April 16, 1984
Adjournment Debate
a question to which I expected a reasonable reply. The question related to the application of Paragraph 231 (l)(c) of the Income Tax Act and the consequential effects of that particular paragraph upon the liberty of the subject. That paragraph permits officers of the Department of National Revenue, in the course of undertaking their investigation, to obtain from taxpayers statements, including statements under oath.
My observation was that, having regard to that provision, there was the real likelihood that a taxpayer who had, in fact, complied with that requirement under Paragraph 231 (l)(c) might later be prosecuted for tax evasion, having made a self-incriminating statement. The response of the Minister is found at page 2335 of Hansard.
In reading the response again, I suspect that never was there a better illustration of why we need these adjournment debates-because of the unsatisfactory nature of the response given to me. The Minister said, and I quote:
-perhaps the Hon. Member would care to examine various provisions of the Income Tax Act which are very specific and reflect the very nature of this legislation and the kind of tax system we have in Canada.
Well, of course, I did examine the provisions of the Income Tax Act. If I had not, I would not have raised the specific issue to the Minister which I did. I would have thought by now, having been in his post as long as he has, the Minister which he is responsible for administering. Yet that does not seem to be the case. He continued by saying:
If he does-
That refers to me.
-he will see that these provisions exist because of the nature of the legislation and the tax system we have in Canada.
It is because of that tax system that I raised that question. I suspect if we were to ask the people of Canada they would almost unanimously agree that the system itself is offensive and should be changed.
One of the offensive provisions is in the very section to which I made reference. I will not read the section, Mr. Speaker, because I briefly explained the intent and purpose of it, but let me read from the Act, under Part XV thereof, which is headed "Administration and Enforcement". The first subsection, 220(1) reads as follows:
The Minister shall administer and enforce this Act and control and supervise all persons employed to carry out or enforce this Act-
It is the Minister of National Revenue, Mr. Speaker, to which reference should be made with respect to administrative provisions, and not the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) who may be responsible for the generation of revenue in the country. Yet this Minister seems to be completely ignorant of the provisions of the very Act for which he is clearly responsible.
What are the implications of Section 231, and in particular, paragraph 231 (l)(c) which, as I indicated, obliges taxpayers to give statements under oath? If one looks further under Part XV one finds under subsection 238(2) the following:
Every person who has failed to comply with or contravened subsection-
And there are a number of subsections listed including subsection 231.
-is guilty of an offence and, in addition to any penalty otherwise provided, is liable on summary conviction to
(a)	a fine of not less than $200 and not exceeding $10,000, or
(b)	both the fine described in paragraph (a) and imprisonment for a term not exceeding 6 months.
Looking further, Mr. Speaker, at paragraph 239(c), for example, it reads:
Every person who has
(c)	made, or assented to or acquiesced in the making of, false or deceptive entries, or omitted, or assented to or acquiesced in the omission, to enter a material particular, in records or books of account of a taxpayer,-
is guilty of an offence and, in addition to any penalty otherwise provided, is liable on summary convictions to
(f)	a fine of not less than 25% and not more than double the amount of the tax that was sought to be evaded, or
(g)	both the fine described in paragraph (f) and imprisonment for a term not exceeding two years.
Then, Mr. Speaker, Section 239(2) says that every person who is charged with an offence described in the Section I just read may, at the election of the Attorney General of Canada, be prosecuted upon indictment and, if convicted, is, in addition to any penalty otherwise provided, liable to imprisonment for a term not exceeding five years and not less than two months.
These are serious matters, Mr. Speaker, not to be taken lightly. We are dealing with the liberty of the individual. When I make reference specifically to an offensive provision in this Act, I do believe that it is appropriate for the Minister responsible for the administration of this Act to stand in his place and give a decent, honest answer. This Section clearly should be amended or repealed so that the liberty of the individual is preserved.

Member for York North (Mr. Gamble) may or may not be aware that the Department of Justice is carefully reviewing the Income Tax Act, as well all other federal statutes to identify possible conflicts with the Charter of Rights. Given this Government's commitment to that Charter, the review is of the most searching kind. I can assure the Hon. Member that Section 231 of the Income Tax Act is included in the review, and I thank him for his interest.
I am well aware of the Hon. Member's expertise in the tax field, and his keen interest in the validity or otherwise of such sections as Section 231 of the Income Tax act is understandable. That having been said, it is not my intention this evening to throw any doubt whatsoever upon the constitutional validity of Section 231 of the Income Tax Act, or any other aspect of the said Act. My intervention this evening is merely to assure

the Hon. Member that the section he referred to will be subject to departmental review.
